subquestions.stem: G1, S, and G2 together make up which broad part of the cell cycle?
subquestions.explanation: Interphase.

subquestions.stem: After S phase, each chromosome consists of two identical ___ joined at a centromere.
subquestions.explanation: Sister chromatids.

free_response.prompt: List the four phases of mitosis in order.
free_response.explanation: Mnemonic 'PMAT': prophase (chromosomes condense), metaphase (align), anaphase (chromatids separate), telophase (nuclei re-form).

source.name: OpenStax Biology 2e — Ch. 10 Cell Reproduction (mitosis)

subquestions.stem: A common mnemonic for the ORDER of the mitosis phases is ___.
subquestions.explanation: PMAT.

subquestions.stem: Division of the cytoplasm, which typically follows mitosis, is called ___.
subquestions.explanation: Cytokinesis.

free_response.prompt: During which phase of mitosis do chromosomes line up single-file along the cell's equator (the metaphase plate)?
free_response.explanation: At metaphase, spindle microtubules align chromosomes at the metaphase plate; the spindle-assembly checkpoint verifies proper attachment before anaphase.

source.name: OpenStax Biology 2e — Ch. 10 Cell Reproduction (mitosis)

subquestions.stem: Spindle fibers attach to a chromosome at a protein structure on its centromere called the ___.
subquestions.explanation: The kinetochore.

subquestions.stem: The checkpoint that confirms all chromosomes are properly attached before anaphase is the ___ checkpoint.
subquestions.explanation: The spindle (M) checkpoint.

free_response.prompt: During which phase of mitosis do SISTER CHROMATIDS separate and move to opposite poles of the cell?
free_response.explanation: In anaphase, cohesin is cleaved and sister chromatids are pulled apart, each becoming an independent chromosome.

source.name: OpenStax Biology 2e — Ch. 10 Cell Reproduction (mitosis)

subquestions.stem: The protein complex holding sister chromatids together (cleaved at anaphase onset) is ___.
subquestions.explanation: Cohesin.

subquestions.stem: Failure of chromatids to separate here leads to ___ (an abnormal chromosome number).
subquestions.explanation: Nondisjunction.

free_response.prompt: What is the name for the division of the CYTOPLASM that typically follows mitosis, producing two separate daughter cells?
free_response.explanation: In animal cells a contractile ring pinches a cleavage furrow; plant cells instead build a cell plate.

source.name: OpenStax Biology 2e — Ch. 10 Cell Reproduction (cytokinesis)

subquestions.stem: In ANIMAL cells, cytokinesis occurs via a pinching ___ furrow.
subquestions.explanation: Cleavage furrow.

subquestions.stem: In PLANT cells, cytokinesis forms a ___ that becomes the new cell wall.
subquestions.explanation: A cell plate.

free_response.prompt: The cell cycle is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases plus regulatory proteins whose levels rise and fall - what are those regulatory proteins called?
free_response.explanation: Cyclins bind and activate CDKs; the cyclin-CDK complexes phosphorylate targets to push the cell through checkpoints.

source.name: OpenStax Biology 2e — Ch. 10 Cell Reproduction (regulation)

subquestions.stem: Cyclins activate which family of enzymes (their partners)?
subquestions.explanation: Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).

subquestions.stem: CDKs regulate their targets by adding what chemical group to them?
subquestions.explanation: A phosphate (phosphorylation).

free_response.prompt: Which tumor-suppressor protein, called the 'guardian of the genome', halts the cell cycle at the G1/S checkpoint when DNA is damaged?
free_response.explanation: p53 arrests the cycle to allow repair, or triggers apoptosis if damage is severe; loss of p53 function is common in cancers.

source.name: OpenStax Biology 2e — Ch. 10 Cancer and the Cell Cycle

subquestions.stem: A gene whose normal role is to RESTRAIN cell division (and whose loss can cause cancer) is a ___ gene.
subquestions.explanation: A tumor-suppressor gene.

subquestions.stem: If DNA damage is too severe to repair, p53 can trigger programmed cell death, called ___.
subquestions.explanation: Apoptosis.

free_response.prompt: What is the term for programmed, controlled cell death (as opposed to injury-induced necrosis)?
free_response.explanation: Apoptosis is orderly, ATP-dependent cell suicide executed by caspases; necrosis is uncontrolled death from injury and causes inflammation.

source.name: OpenStax Biology 2e — Ch. 9-10 Cell communication / cell cycle

subquestions.stem: Which family of proteases executes apoptosis?
subquestions.explanation: Caspases.

subquestions.stem: Uncontrolled, injury-induced cell death that causes inflammation is called ___.
subquestions.explanation: Necrosis.

free_response.prompt: What term describes a stem cell that can give rise to ALL cell types of the body PLUS extraembryonic tissue (like the zygote)?
free_response.explanation: Totipotent (zygote) -> any cell including placenta; pluripotent (embryonic stem cells) -> any body cell but not placenta; multipotent -> limited lineages.

source.name: OpenStax Biology 2e — Ch. 43 (development) / stem cells

subquestions.stem: A stem cell that can form any cell of the body but NOT extraembryonic tissue is called ___.
subquestions.explanation: Pluripotent.

subquestions.stem: A stem cell limited to a few related cell types (e.g., blood cells) is called ___.
subquestions.explanation: Multipotent.

free_response.prompt: What is the process by which an unspecialized cell becomes specialized in structure and function (mostly via differential gene expression)?
free_response.explanation: Different cell types share the same genome but express different genes; differentiation is driven by regulated gene expression, not by losing genes.

source.name: OpenStax Biology 2e — Ch. 16 Gene Regulation (differentiation)

subquestions.stem: Do differentiated cells in your body generally have the SAME or DIFFERENT genomes?
subquestions.explanation: The same genome.

subquestions.stem: Differentiation results mainly from differences in ___ among cells.
subquestions.explanation: Gene expression.

free_response.prompt: Cancer arises fundamentally from a loss of control over what cellular process?
free_response.model_answer: Cell division (loss of cell-cycle control -> uncontrolled proliferation)
free_response.explanation: Mutations in proto-oncogenes (gain of function) and tumor-suppressor genes (loss of function) release the brakes on cell division.

source.name: OpenStax Biology 2e — Ch. 10 Cancer and the Cell Cycle

subquestions.stem: A mutated, OVERACTIVE gene that promotes cancerous growth is called an ___.
subquestions.explanation: An oncogene.

subquestions.stem: The normal, un-mutated version of such a growth-promoting gene is called a ___.
subquestions.explanation: A proto-oncogene.

free_response.prompt: What is the approximate resting membrane potential of a typical neuron (value with sign and unit)?
free_response.explanation: The inside of a resting neuron is negative relative to the outside (~-70 mV), set mainly by K+ permeability and the Na+/K+ pump.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 12 The Nervous System (membrane potential)

subquestions.stem: Is the inside of a resting neuron negative or positive relative to the outside?
subquestions.explanation: Negative.

subquestions.stem: At rest, the membrane is MOST permeable to which ion (via leak channels)?
subquestions.explanation: Potassium (K+).

free_response.prompt: Which membrane pump uses ATP to maintain the Na+ and K+ gradients essential for the resting potential?
free_response.explanation: It pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP, sustaining the gradients that set the resting potential and power secondary active transport.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 12 The Nervous System

subquestions.stem: How many Na+ does the pump export per cycle?
subquestions.explanation: 3 Na+ out.

subquestions.stem: How many K+ does the pump import per cycle?
subquestions.explanation: 2 K+ in.

free_response.prompt: The rapid rising (depolarizing) phase of a neuronal action potential is caused by the INFLUX of which ion?
free_response.explanation: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open at threshold, letting Na+ rush in and depolarize the membrane toward about +30 mV.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 12 The Action Potential

subquestions.stem: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open when the membrane reaches its ___ (a critical voltage).
subquestions.explanation: Threshold.

subquestions.stem: An action potential either fires fully or not at all - this is the ___ principle.
subquestions.explanation: All-or-none.

free_response.prompt: The falling (repolarizing) phase of the action potential is caused by the EFFLUX of which ion?
free_response.explanation: Voltage-gated K+ channels open (more slowly) and K+ leaves, restoring negativity; a brief overshoot causes hyperpolarization.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 12 The Action Potential

subquestions.stem: A brief dip BELOW the resting potential after the spike is called ___.
subquestions.explanation: Hyperpolarization.

subquestions.stem: During the ___ period, the neuron cannot fire another action potential.
subquestions.explanation: The refractory period.

free_response.prompt: Which glial cell forms the myelin sheath around axons in the CENTRAL nervous system?
free_response.explanation: In the CNS, oligodendrocytes myelinate axons; in the PNS, Schwann cells do.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 12 Nervous Tissue (glia)

subquestions.stem: Which cell myelinates axons in the PERIPHERAL nervous system (PNS)?
subquestions.explanation: Schwann cells.

subquestions.stem: Myelin increases conduction speed by letting the impulse jump between nodes - this is ___ conduction.
subquestions.explanation: Saltatory conduction.

free_response.prompt: What are the periodic gaps in the myelin sheath, where the action potential is regenerated, called?
free_response.explanation: Action potentials 'jump' from node to node (saltatory conduction), greatly speeding transmission along myelinated axons.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 12 Nervous Tissue (myelin)

subquestions.stem: The jumping of the action potential from node to node is called ___ conduction.
subquestions.explanation: Saltatory conduction.

subquestions.stem: Does myelination INCREASE or DECREASE the speed of conduction?
subquestions.explanation: Increases speed.

free_response.prompt: What general term describes the chemical messengers released from an axon terminal into the synaptic cleft to signal the next cell?
free_response.explanation: Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind receptors on the postsynaptic membrane; examples include acetylcholine, dopamine, and glutamate.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 12 The Synapse

subquestions.stem: The gap between two neurons across which neurotransmitters diffuse is the synaptic ___.
subquestions.explanation: The synaptic cleft.

subquestions.stem: Neurotransmitter release is triggered by the influx of which ion into the axon terminal?
subquestions.explanation: Calcium (Ca2+).

free_response.prompt: Which neurotransmitter is released at the NEUROMUSCULAR junction to trigger skeletal muscle contraction?
free_response.explanation: ACh binds nicotinic receptors on the muscle fiber; acetylcholinesterase then degrades it to terminate the signal.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 11 Muscle Tissue (NMJ)

subquestions.stem: Which enzyme breaks down acetylcholine in the cleft to end the signal?
subquestions.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase.

subquestions.stem: The junction between a motor neuron and a muscle fiber is called the ___ junction.
subquestions.explanation: The neuromuscular junction.

free_response.prompt: Which division of the autonomic nervous system mediates the 'fight-or-flight' response?
free_response.explanation: Sympathetic activation raises heart rate, dilates the pupils, and mobilizes energy; the parasympathetic division does the opposite ('rest and digest').

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 15 The Autonomic Nervous System

subquestions.stem: Which division mediates the 'rest-and-digest' response?
subquestions.explanation: The parasympathetic nervous system.

subquestions.stem: Does sympathetic activation RAISE or LOWER heart rate?
subquestions.explanation: Raises heart rate.

free_response.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries most PARASYMPATHETIC output to the heart and abdominal viscera?
free_response.explanation: The vagus provides parasympathetic innervation that slows the heart and stimulates digestion, releasing acetylcholine at its targets.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 15 Autonomic Nervous System (vagus)

subquestions.stem: The main neurotransmitter of parasympathetic postganglionic neurons is ___.
subquestions.explanation: Acetylcholine.

subquestions.stem: Does vagal (parasympathetic) activity speed up or slow down the heart?
subquestions.explanation: Slows the heart.

free_response.prompt: Which endocrine gland, often called the 'master gland', is directly controlled by the hypothalamus?
free_response.explanation: The anterior pituitary secretes hormones (TSH, ACTH, FSH/LH, GH) under hypothalamic releasing hormones; the posterior pituitary stores/releases ADH and oxytocin made by the hypothalamus.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 17 The Endocrine System (pituitary)

subquestions.stem: Which brain region controls the pituitary and links the nervous and endocrine systems?
subquestions.explanation: The hypothalamus.

subquestions.stem: The posterior pituitary releases ADH and which other hypothalamic hormone?
subquestions.explanation: Oxytocin.

free_response.prompt: Steroid hormones (being lipid-soluble) typically bind receptors located WHERE in/on the target cell?
free_response.explanation: Lipid-soluble steroids cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors; water-soluble peptide hormones bind cell-surface receptors and use second messengers.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 17 Endocrine System (hormone signaling)

subquestions.stem: Peptide hormones bind receptors located WHERE (since they cannot cross the membrane)?
subquestions.explanation: On the cell surface (plasma membrane).

subquestions.stem: Peptide-hormone signaling often uses an intracellular 'second messenger' such as ___.
subquestions.explanation: cAMP (or Ca2+/IP3).

free_response.prompt: Which hormone RAISES blood calcium (e.g., by stimulating bone resorption and renal Ca2+ reabsorption)?
free_response.explanation: PTH raises blood Ca2+; calcitonin (from the thyroid) lowers it. The two are antagonists regulating calcium homeostasis.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 17 Endocrine System (calcium homeostasis)

subquestions.stem: Which hormone LOWERS blood calcium, opposing PTH?
subquestions.explanation: Calcitonin.

subquestions.stem: PTH is secreted by which glands?
subquestions.explanation: The parathyroid glands.

free_response.prompt: Which posterior-pituitary hormone promotes water reabsorption in the kidney's collecting ducts, concentrating the urine?
free_response.explanation: ADH inserts aquaporins into the collecting duct so more water is reabsorbed; alcohol inhibits ADH, causing diuresis.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 17 / Ch. 25 (ADH and the kidney)

subquestions.stem: ADH increases water reabsorption by inserting water channels called ___ into the membrane.
subquestions.explanation: Aquaporins.

subquestions.stem: Does ADH make the urine MORE concentrated or MORE dilute?
subquestions.explanation: More concentrated.

free_response.prompt: Rising blood thyroid hormone inhibits the release of TSH and TRH. What is this regulatory pattern called?
free_response.explanation: Most endocrine axes use negative feedback: the product inhibits its own upstream stimulators, keeping levels stable. Positive feedback (e.g., oxytocin in labor) is rarer.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 17 Endocrine System (feedback)

subquestions.stem: Give one example of a POSITIVE feedback loop in human physiology.
subquestions.explanation: Oxytocin during labor (also the LH surge, or clotting).

subquestions.stem: Negative feedback holds a variable near a stable set point; this overall stability is called ___.
subquestions.explanation: Homeostasis.

free_response.prompt: Which hormone, secreted by the adrenal MEDULLA, reinforces the sympathetic 'fight-or-flight' response?
free_response.explanation: The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine (and norepinephrine) into the blood, prolonging sympathetic effects such as increased heart rate and glucose mobilization.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 17 Endocrine System (adrenal gland)

subquestions.stem: The adrenal ___ (outer region) instead secretes steroid hormones like cortisol and aldosterone.
subquestions.explanation: The adrenal cortex.

subquestions.stem: Epinephrine is an amine/peptide-type hormone, so it binds receptors located where on the target cell?
subquestions.explanation: The cell surface.

free_response.prompt: What is the term for the neural pathway that produces a rapid, involuntary motor response to a stimulus, often without initial brain involvement?
free_response.explanation: A simple reflex arc runs sensory (afferent) neuron -> (interneuron) -> motor (efferent) neuron; a monosynaptic reflex (e.g., knee-jerk) skips the interneuron.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 13 The Spinal Cord and Reflexes

subquestions.stem: Neurons carrying signals TOWARD the CNS are called ___ (sensory) neurons.
subquestions.explanation: Afferent (sensory) neurons.

subquestions.stem: Neurons carrying signals AWAY from the CNS to effectors are called ___ (motor) neurons.
subquestions.explanation: Efferent (motor) neurons.

free_response.prompt: The central nervous system (CNS) consists of which two structures?
free_response.model_answer: The brain and the spinal cord
free_response.explanation: The CNS is the brain plus the spinal cord; everything else (cranial/spinal nerves, ganglia) is the peripheral nervous system (PNS).

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 12 The Nervous System (organization)

subquestions.stem: All neural tissue OUTSIDE the brain and spinal cord makes up which system?
subquestions.explanation: The peripheral nervous system (PNS).

subquestions.stem: Is the autonomic nervous system a subdivision of the CNS or the PNS?
subquestions.explanation: The PNS.

free_response.prompt: When several excitatory postsynaptic potentials add together (over time or space) to reach threshold, this process is called what?
free_response.explanation: Temporal summation = rapid inputs from one synapse; spatial summation = simultaneous inputs from many synapses. Together they decide whether the neuron fires.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 12 The Synapse (integration)

subquestions.stem: Summation of inputs arriving in quick succession at ONE synapse is ___ summation.
subquestions.explanation: Temporal summation.

subquestions.stem: Summation of inputs from MANY synapses at once is ___ summation.
subquestions.explanation: Spatial summation.

free_response.prompt: Oxygenated blood returning from the lungs via the pulmonary veins enters which chamber of the heart FIRST?
free_response.explanation: Path: pulmonary veins -> left atrium -> left ventricle -> aorta -> body. Uniquely, the pulmonary veins carry OXYGENATED blood.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 19 The Heart (blood flow)

subquestions.stem: From the left atrium, blood next passes into which chamber?
subquestions.explanation: The left ventricle.

subquestions.stem: Do the pulmonary VEINS carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
subquestions.explanation: Oxygenated (an exception to the usual vein rule).

free_response.prompt: Which heart chamber pumps oxygenated blood out to the ENTIRE body through the aorta?
free_response.explanation: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must generate the high pressure needed to drive systemic circulation.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 19 The Heart (chambers)

subquestions.stem: Why does the left ventricle have a THICKER muscular wall than the right?
subquestions.explanation: It must generate higher pressure for the systemic circuit.

subquestions.stem: The large artery leaving the left ventricle is the ___.
subquestions.explanation: The aorta.

free_response.prompt: What is the name of the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle?
free_response.explanation: The mitral valve is the left AV valve; the tricuspid is the right AV valve. The semilunar valves (aortic, pulmonary) guard the ventricular outflows.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 19 The Heart (valves)

subquestions.stem: What is the valve between the right atrium and right ventricle called?
subquestions.explanation: The tricuspid valve.

subquestions.stem: The valves at the exits of the ventricles (aortic and pulmonary) are called ___ valves.
subquestions.explanation: Semilunar valves.

free_response.prompt: Which structure serves as the natural PACEMAKER of the heart, initiating each heartbeat?
free_response.explanation: The SA node in the right atrium sets the rhythm; the impulse then spreads to the AV node, bundle of His, and Purkinje fibers.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 19 The Heart (conduction system)

subquestions.stem: After the SA node, the impulse is briefly delayed at which node before reaching the ventricles?
subquestions.explanation: The atrioventricular (AV) node.

subquestions.stem: Fibers that rapidly spread the impulse through the ventricular walls are the ___ fibers.
subquestions.explanation: Purkinje fibers.

free_response.prompt: Which oxygen-binding protein in red blood cells transports most of the oxygen in the blood?
free_response.explanation: Each hemoglobin binds up to four O2 at its iron-containing heme groups; most blood O2 is carried this way, not dissolved in plasma.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 18 The Blood (erythrocytes)

subquestions.stem: Which metal ion in the heme group of hemoglobin actually binds oxygen?
subquestions.explanation: Iron (Fe2+).

subquestions.stem: How many O2 molecules can one hemoglobin carry at full saturation?
subquestions.explanation: Four.

free_response.prompt: In the lungs, gas exchange between air and blood occurs across the walls of which tiny sac-like structures?
free_response.explanation: Alveoli provide a huge, thin surface for O2/CO2 diffusion between air and the surrounding pulmonary capillaries.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 22 The Respiratory System (alveoli)

subquestions.stem: Gas exchange occurs by simple ___ across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane.
subquestions.explanation: Diffusion.

subquestions.stem: A detergent-like substance that reduces surface tension and keeps alveoli open is called ___.
subquestions.explanation: Surfactant.

free_response.prompt: Which dome-shaped skeletal muscle is the primary driver of inhalation (contracting and flattening to expand the chest)?
free_response.explanation: When the diaphragm contracts (flattens), thoracic volume rises and pressure falls, drawing air in (Boyle's law); relaxation drives passive exhalation.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 22 Respiratory System (ventilation)

subquestions.stem: When the diaphragm contracts, does lung volume increase or decrease?
subquestions.explanation: Increases (air flows in).

subquestions.stem: Contracting the diaphragm ___ the intrapulmonary pressure (per Boyle's law), so air flows in.
subquestions.explanation: Lowers it below atmospheric pressure.

free_response.prompt: In what chemical form is the MAJORITY of carbon dioxide transported in the blood?
free_response.explanation: About 70% of CO2 travels as HCO3- (formed via carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells); the rest binds hemoglobin (carbaminohemoglobin) or is dissolved.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 22 Respiratory System (gas transport)

subquestions.stem: Which enzyme in red blood cells converts CO2 + H2O into carbonic acid/bicarbonate?
subquestions.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase.

subquestions.stem: CO2 bound directly to hemoglobin forms ___.
subquestions.explanation: Carbaminohemoglobin.

free_response.prompt: What is the functional unit of the kidney, where blood is filtered and urine is formed?
free_response.explanation: Each kidney has about a million nephrons; each has a glomerulus (filter) and a tubule (reabsorption/secretion).

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 25 The Urinary System (nephron)

subquestions.stem: The tuft of capillaries where blood is filtered at the start of the nephron is the ___.
subquestions.explanation: The glomerulus.

subquestions.stem: The three basic renal processes are filtration, reabsorption, and ___.
subquestions.explanation: Secretion.

free_response.prompt: In a healthy nephron, essentially ALL filtered glucose is reabsorbed in which segment?
free_response.explanation: The PCT reabsorbs glucose (via Na+-glucose symport), amino acids, and most water and ions; glucose appears in urine only when these transporters are saturated (as in diabetes).

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 25 The Urinary System (reabsorption)

subquestions.stem: Glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT by cotransport coupled to which ion?
subquestions.explanation: Sodium (Na+) - via SGLT symport.

subquestions.stem: Glucose appears in the urine when these transporters become ___ (as in untreated diabetes).
subquestions.explanation: Saturated (the transport maximum is exceeded).

free_response.prompt: Which enzyme, secreted in the stomach and active at low pH, BEGINS the digestion of proteins?
free_response.explanation: Pepsin is secreted as inactive pepsinogen and activated by stomach acid (HCl); it works best at about pH 2.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 23 The Digestive System (stomach)

subquestions.stem: Pepsin is secreted in an inactive precursor form called ___.
subquestions.explanation: Pepsinogen.

subquestions.stem: Which acid, secreted by parietal cells, activates pepsin and denatures proteins?
subquestions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid (HCl).

free_response.prompt: In which organ does the MAJORITY of nutrient absorption occur?
free_response.explanation: The small intestine's villi and microvilli create an enormous absorptive surface area; its first segment is the duodenum.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 23 The Digestive System (small intestine)

subquestions.stem: Finger-like projections that increase absorptive surface area in the small intestine are ___.
subquestions.explanation: Villi (and microvilli).

subquestions.stem: The first segment of the small intestine, receiving stomach contents, is the ___.
subquestions.explanation: The duodenum.

free_response.prompt: Which substance, produced by the LIVER, emulsifies fats to aid their digestion and absorption?
free_response.explanation: Bile (made by the liver, stored in the gallbladder) emulsifies large fat globules into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 23 Digestive System (liver, gallbladder)

subquestions.stem: Bile is stored and concentrated in which organ before release?
subquestions.explanation: The gallbladder.

subquestions.stem: Does bile chemically DIGEST fat, or physically EMULSIFY it?
subquestions.explanation: It emulsifies (physically); lipase does the chemical digestion.

free_response.prompt: Which pancreatic enzyme digests carbohydrates (starch) in the small intestine?
free_response.explanation: Amylase breaks starch into maltose/disaccharides; the pancreas also secretes proteases (trypsin) and lipase, plus bicarbonate to neutralize stomach acid.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 23 Digestive System (pancreas)

subquestions.stem: Which pancreatic enzyme digests fats?
subquestions.explanation: Lipase.

subquestions.stem: What does the pancreas secrete to NEUTRALIZE the acidic chyme entering the small intestine?
subquestions.explanation: Bicarbonate.

free_response.prompt: Which lymphocytes produce ANTIBODIES as part of the humoral (antibody-mediated) immune response?
free_response.model_answer: B cells (which differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells)
free_response.explanation: Activated B cells become plasma cells that secrete antibodies; some become memory B cells for a faster future response.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 21 The Immune System (adaptive)

subquestions.stem: Antibody-secreting effector B cells are specifically called ___ cells.
subquestions.explanation: Plasma cells.

subquestions.stem: Long-lived cells enabling a faster response on re-exposure are ___ cells.
subquestions.explanation: Memory cells.

free_response.prompt: Which lymphocytes are central to CELL-MEDIATED immunity, including directly killing infected cells (cytotoxic) and coordinating the response (helper)?
free_response.explanation: Cytotoxic (CD8+) T cells kill infected/abnormal cells; helper (CD4+) T cells activate B cells and other immune cells. HIV targets CD4+ helper T cells.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 21 The Immune System (T cells)

subquestions.stem: Which T-cell subtype directly DESTROYS virus-infected or cancerous cells?
subquestions.explanation: Cytotoxic (CD8+) T cells.

subquestions.stem: Which T-cell subtype (targeted by HIV) COORDINATES the immune response by activating other cells?
subquestions.explanation: Helper (CD4+) T cells.

free_response.prompt: Which branch of immunity is nonspecific, rapid, and present from birth (e.g., skin, phagocytes, inflammation)?
free_response.explanation: Innate immunity is fast and nonspecific (barriers, phagocytes, inflammation); adaptive immunity is slower, specific, and has memory (B and T cells).

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 21 The Immune System (innate vs adaptive)

subquestions.stem: Which branch of immunity is SPECIFIC and develops immunological memory?
subquestions.explanation: Adaptive (acquired) immunity.

subquestions.stem: Which white blood cells 'eat' pathogens by phagocytosis in the innate response?
subquestions.explanation: Phagocytes (macrophages, neutrophils).

free_response.prompt: What is the name of the basic contractile unit of a skeletal muscle fiber, the region between two Z lines?
free_response.explanation: Sarcomeres (Z line to Z line) contain overlapping thin (actin) and thick (myosin) filaments; their shortening produces contraction.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 10 Muscle Tissue (sarcomere)

subquestions.stem: A sarcomere is bounded on each side by which structure/line?
subquestions.explanation: The Z lines (Z discs).

subquestions.stem: During contraction, do the filaments themselves shorten, or slide past each other?
subquestions.explanation: They slide past each other.

free_response.prompt: Name the two protein filaments whose interaction produces muscle contraction (the thin and the thick filaments).
free_response.explanation: Per the sliding-filament model, myosin heads bind actin and pull it inward, shortening the sarcomere; this requires ATP and Ca2+.

source.name: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Ch. 10 Muscle Tissue (contraction)

subquestions.stem: Which is the THICK filament - actin or myosin?
subquestions.explanation: Myosin.

subquestions.stem: The model in which filaments slide past one another is the ___ theory.

free_response.prompt: Which bone cells are responsible for BUILDING new bone matrix (bone formation)?

free_response.prompt: A mid-cycle SURGE of which hormone triggers ovulation (release of the egg from the ovary)?

free_response.prompt: What is the term for the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes?

free_response.prompt: What is the normal pH range of human ARTERIAL blood?

free_response.prompt: A ball is released from rest and falls freely for 3.0 s (g = 10 m/s², neglect air resistance). What is its speed just before landing? Give the value with units.
free_response.explanation: From rest v₀ = 0, so speed grows linearly as v = g t. The distance fallen (½ g t² = 45 m) is a common trap; it is a length, not a speed.

subquestions.explanation: "Released from rest" means v₀ = 0.

free_response.prompt: A marble rolls off a table 1.25 m high with a horizontal speed of 3.0 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). How far from the base of the table does it land? Give the value with units.

subquestions.explanation: No horizontal force means aₓ = 0, so vₓ is constant.

subquestions.explanation: t = √(2h/g) = √0.25 = 0.50 s; time aloft depends only on the drop height.

free_response.prompt: A constant net force gives a 2.0 kg cart an acceleration of 3.0 m/s². What is the magnitude of the net force? Give the value with units.
free_response.model_answer: Newton's second law: F_net = m a = (2.0 kg)(3.0 m/s²) = 6.0 N.
free_response.explanation: Force equals mass times acceleration; the newton is kg·m/s².

subquestions.stem: State Newton's second law relating net force, mass, and acceleration.
subquestions.explanation: F_net = m a.

subquestions.stem: Evaluate (2.0 kg)(3.0 m/s²) (give N).

subquestions.explanation: a = F/m = 6.0/4.0 = 1.5 m/s²; doubling mass halves acceleration.

free_response.prompt: A 10 kg crate slides across a level floor with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.30 (g = 10 m/s²). What horizontal force keeps it moving at constant velocity? Give the value with units.
free_response.model_answer: At constant velocity a = 0, so applied force = kinetic friction. N = mg = (10)(10) = 100 N, so f_k = μ_k N = (0.30)(100) = 30 N.
free_response.explanation: Kinetic friction is μ_k times the normal force; on a level floor the normal force equals the weight.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 5: Further Applications of Newton's Laws: Friction

subquestions.stem: For a crate on a horizontal floor, what does the normal force equal (in N)?
subquestions.explanation: Vertical equilibrium gives N = mg = (10)(10) = 100 N.

subquestions.stem: Write the equation for kinetic friction in terms of μ_k and N.
subquestions.explanation: Kinetic friction equals the coefficient times the normal force.

subquestions.stem: Compute (0.30)(100 N) (give N).
subquestions.explanation: f_k = (0.30)(100) = 30 N, which balances the applied force at constant velocity.

free_response.prompt: A block is released from rest on a frictionless incline angled 30° above the horizontal (g = 10 m/s²). What is its acceleration down the incline? Give the value with units.
free_response.model_answer: Along a frictionless incline a = g sinθ = (10)(sin 30°) = (10)(0.50) = 5.0 m/s².
free_response.explanation: Only the component of gravity parallel to the surface accelerates the block; that component is g sinθ.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 4-5: Newton's Laws / Inclined planes

subquestions.stem: What component of gravitational acceleration acts along a frictionless incline of angle θ?
subquestions.explanation: The parallel component is g sinθ; the perpendicular component g cosθ is balanced by the normal force.

free_response.prompt: On a seesaw pivoted at its center, a 300 N child sits 1.0 m left of the pivot. How far right of the pivot must a 200 N child sit to balance it? Give the distance with units.
free_response.model_answer: Balance requires equal and opposite torques: (300 N)(1.0 m) = (200 N)(d) → d = 300/200 = 1.5 m.
free_response.explanation: Static equilibrium means net torque = 0. Torque is force × lever arm, so the lighter child must sit farther out.

subquestions.stem: For a balanced seesaw, what must be true of the net torque about the pivot?
subquestions.explanation: Rotational equilibrium requires the clockwise and counterclockwise torques to be equal (net torque zero).

subquestions.explanation: Torque = force × distance on each side: (300)(1.0) = (200)(d).

free_response.prompt: A worker pushes a box 4.0 m across the floor with a constant 25 N force directed along the motion. How much work does the worker do? Give the value with units.

free_response.prompt: An object is dropped from rest at a height of 5.0 m (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance). What is its speed just before it hits the ground? Give the value with units.
free_response.model_answer: Energy conservation: mgh = ½ m v² → v = √(2 g h) = √(2·10·5.0) = √100 = 10 m/s.

free_response.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball moving at 4.0 m/s is brought to rest. What is the magnitude of the impulse delivered to the ball? Give the value with units.
free_response.model_answer: Impulse equals the change in momentum: J = Δp = mΔv = (0.50)(4.0 − 0) = 2.0 kg·m/s (equivalently 2.0 N·s).
free_response.explanation: Impulse and momentum share units: kg·m/s = N·s. Stopping the ball removes all of its momentum.

free_response.prompt: In a hydraulic lift, the input piston has area 0.010 m² and the output piston has area 0.10 m². If 50 N is applied to the input, what force appears at the output? Give the value with units.

free_response.prompt: An incompressible fluid flows at 2.0 m/s through a pipe. Where the pipe's cross-sectional area is half as large, what is the fluid speed? Give the value with units.

free_response.explanation: Bernoulli's equation conserves energy per unit volume; faster-moving fluid carries more of its energy as kinetic energy, leaving less as pressure.

subquestions.stem: Compute (2.0)(3.0)(4.0) (give N).
If the charge moved PARALLEL to B instead, what would the force be?
subquestions.explanation: F = qvB sinθ = 0 when v ∥ B (θ = 0).

free_response.prompt: For a galvanic cell with a Cu²⁺/Cu cathode (E° = +0.34 V) and a Zn²⁺/Zn anode (E° = −0.76 V), what is the standard cell potential? Give the value with units.
free_response.explanation: A positive E°_cell means the reaction is spontaneous as written (ΔG° = −nFE°_cell < 0).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 17: Electrochemistry — Standard Cell Potentials

subquestions.stem: Write the formula for standard cell potential from electrode potentials.
subquestions.explanation: E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode.
Subtracting a negative adds: 0.34 + 0.76 = 1.10 V.

subquestions.stem: Is a cell with E°_cell = +1.10 V spontaneous? (yes/no)
subquestions.explanation: Positive E°_cell ↔ negative ΔG° ↔ spontaneous.

free_response.prompt: How many coulombs of charge are required to deposit 1.0 mol of silver from Ag⁺ (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag)? Use F = 96,485 C/mol. Give the value with units.
free_response.model_answer: Depositing 1 mol Ag needs 1 mol of electrons: Q = nF = (1)(96,485) ≈ 9.65×10⁴ C.
free_response.explanation: Faraday's law links moles of electrons to charge; one mole of electrons carries one faraday (96,485 C).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 17: Electrochemistry — Electrolysis

subquestions.stem: How many moles of electrons are needed per mole of Ag⁺ reduced?
subquestions.explanation: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag uses 1 mol e⁻ per mol Ag.

subquestions.stem: What is the Faraday constant (charge per mole of electrons)?
Compute Q = (1 mol)(96,485 C/mol) (give C).

free_response.prompt: How much work is required to move a +2.0 C charge through a potential difference of +5.0 V? Give the value with units.
free_response.explanation: The change in electric potential energy equals charge times potential difference (ΔU = qΔV).

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 19: Electric Potential and Electric Field

subquestions.stem: Write the relationship between work/energy, charge, and potential difference.
subquestions.explanation: W = qΔV (= ΔU).

subquestions.stem: Compute (2.0 C)(5.0 V) (give J).
One volt equals one joule per what unit of charge?

free_response.prompt: A copper wire has resistivity 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, length 2.0 m, and cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². What is its resistance? Give the value with units.
free_response.explanation: Resistance rises with length and falls with cross-sectional area; resistivity is the material property.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 20: Electric Current, Resistance, and Ohm's Law

subquestions.stem: Write the equation for the resistance of a uniform wire.
subquestions.explanation: R = ρL/A.

subquestions.stem: Doubling the wire's cross-sectional area would do what to its resistance?
subquestions.explanation: R ∝ 1/A, so doubling A halves R.

free_response.prompt: A sound wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. What is its speed? Give the value with units.
free_response.explanation: The wave equation v = fλ ties speed, frequency, and wavelength; 340 m/s is roughly the speed of sound in air.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 16: Oscillatory Motion and Waves

subquestions.stem: Write the wave equation relating speed, frequency, and wavelength.
subquestions.explanation: v = fλ.

subquestions.stem: Compute (500 Hz)(0.68 m) (give m/s).
If frequency doubles at constant wave speed, what happens to wavelength?
subquestions.explanation: v is fixed, so λ = v/f halves when f doubles.

free_response.prompt: A sound has intensity 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ W/m². Using I₀ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² W/m², what is its sound intensity level? Give the value in decibels.
free_response.explanation: The decibel scale is logarithmic: each factor-of-10 increase in intensity adds 10 dB.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 17: Physics of Hearing

subquestions.stem: Write the formula for sound intensity level in decibels.
subquestions.explanation: β = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀).

subquestions.stem: Compute the ratio I/I₀ = 10⁻⁶ / 10⁻¹².
Evaluate 10 log(10⁶) (give dB).
subquestions.explanation: log(10⁶) = 6, so β = 60 dB.

free_response.prompt: A sound source moves toward a stationary observer. Is the frequency the observer hears higher or lower than the emitted frequency? Answer in one word.
free_response.model_answer: Higher. Motion toward the observer compresses the wavefronts, shortening the wavelength and raising the observed frequency.
free_response.explanation: The Doppler effect shifts perceived frequency up for approach and down for recession; it underlies the changing pitch of a passing siren.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 17: Physics of Hearing — Doppler Effect

subquestions.stem: When the source approaches, what happens to the spacing (wavelength) of the wavefronts ahead of it?
subquestions.explanation: The wavefronts pile up, shortening the wavelength.

subquestions.stem: At fixed wave speed, a shorter wavelength corresponds to a higher or lower frequency?
subquestions.explanation: f = v/λ, so shorter λ means higher f.

subquestions.stem: Therefore the observed pitch is ____ than emitted. (one word)
subquestions.explanation: Approach → higher pitch.

free_response.prompt: A string fixed at both ends is 1.0 m long, and waves travel on it at 200 m/s. What is the fundamental frequency? Give the value with units.
free_response.model_answer: For a string fixed at both ends the fundamental wavelength is λ₁ = 2L = 2.0 m, so f₁ = v/λ₁ = 200/2.0 = 100 Hz.
free_response.explanation: The fundamental fits half a wavelength between the fixed ends; higher harmonics are integer multiples of f₁.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 16: Oscillatory Motion and Waves — Standing Waves

subquestions.stem: For a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental wavelength equals how many times the length L?
subquestions.explanation: λ₁ = 2L (half a wavelength spans the string).

subquestions.stem: Compute λ₁ = 2L for L = 1.0 m (give m).
Compute f₁ = v/λ₁ = 200/2.0 (give Hz).

free_response.prompt: Which has more energy per photon: an X-ray or a radio wave? Answer with the type of radiation.
free_response.model_answer: X-ray. Photon energy E = hf increases with frequency, and X-rays have a far higher frequency than radio waves.
free_response.explanation: Across the EM spectrum, higher frequency (shorter wavelength) means higher photon energy: radio < IR < visible < UV < X-ray < gamma.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 24: Electromagnetic Waves

subquestions.stem: Write the equation for the energy of a single photon.
subquestions.explanation: E = hf, where h is Planck's constant.

subquestions.stem: Which has the higher frequency, X-rays or radio waves?
subquestions.explanation: X-rays have a much higher frequency than radio waves.

subquestions.stem: Higher frequency therefore means higher or lower photon energy?
subquestions.explanation: E ∝ f, so higher frequency → higher energy → X-rays win.

free_response.prompt: Light passes from air (n = 1.0) into glass (n = 1.5) with an angle of incidence of 30°. What is the angle of refraction? Give the value in degrees.
free_response.model_answer: Snell's law: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂ → sinθ₂ = (1.0)(sin 30°)/1.5 = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333, so θ₂ = arcsin(0.333) ≈ 19.5°.
free_response.explanation: Light bends toward the normal when entering a denser (higher-n) medium, so the refracted angle is smaller than the incident angle.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 25: Geometric Optics — The Law of Refraction

subquestions.stem: State Snell's law of refraction.
subquestions.explanation: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂.

subquestions.stem: Solve for sinθ₂ with n₁ = 1.0, θ₁ = 30°, n₂ = 1.5.
Take arcsin(0.333) (give degrees).

free_response.prompt: For light traveling from glass (n = 1.5) toward air (n = 1.0), what is the critical angle for total internal reflection? Give the value in degrees.
free_response.model_answer: At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes at 90°: sinθ_c = n₂/n₁ = 1.0/1.5 = 0.667, so θ_c = arcsin(0.667) ≈ 41.8°.
free_response.explanation: Total internal reflection occurs only going from a denser to a less dense medium, above the critical angle — the basis of fiber optics.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 25: Geometric Optics — Total Internal Reflection

subquestions.stem: At the critical angle, what is the angle of refraction?
subquestions.explanation: The refracted ray travels along the surface at 90°.

subquestions.stem: Write the equation for the critical angle (from medium 1 to medium 2).
subquestions.explanation: sinθ_c = n₂/n₁.

subquestions.stem: Compute arcsin(1.0/1.5) (give degrees).

free_response.prompt: An object is placed 15 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image formed? Give the image distance with units.
free_response.explanation: A positive image distance means a real image forms on the opposite side of the lens.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 25: Geometric Optics — Thin Lenses

subquestions.stem: Write the thin lens equation.
Solve for 1/dᵢ with f = 10 cm and dₒ = 15 cm.
Invert 1/dᵢ = 1/30 to find dᵢ (give cm).
subquestions.explanation: dᵢ = 30 cm.

free_response.prompt: For the lens above (image distance 30 cm, object distance 15 cm), what is the magnification (include sign)? Give the numeric value.
free_response.model_answer: m = −dᵢ/dₒ = −30/15 = −2. The negative sign indicates an inverted image, twice the object's size.
free_response.explanation: Magnification magnitude is the size ratio; a negative sign denotes an inverted (real) image.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 25: Geometric Optics — Image Formation

subquestions.stem: Write the magnification formula in terms of image and object distances.
subquestions.explanation: m = −dᵢ/dₒ.

subquestions.stem: Compute −30/15.
What does the negative sign tell you about the image orientation?
subquestions.explanation: A negative magnification means the image is inverted.

free_response.prompt: In an IR spectrum, a strong absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ is the signature of which bond? Give the bond.
free_response.model_answer: C=O (the carbonyl group). The strong stretch near 1700 cm⁻¹ identifies aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, and amides.
free_response.explanation: IR absorptions arise from bond-stretching vibrations; the carbonyl gives one of the strongest, most diagnostic IR peaks.

source.name: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, Ch. 12: Structure Determination — Infrared Spectroscopy

subquestions.stem: IR absorptions are caused by what kind of molecular motion?
subquestions.explanation: IR light excites bond vibrations (stretching and bending).

subquestions.stem: A strong, sharp peak near 1700 cm⁻¹ is characteristic of which functional feature?
subquestions.explanation: The ~1700 cm⁻¹ band is the carbonyl (C=O) stretch.

subquestions.stem: Name one functional group that contains a C=O and shows this peak.
subquestions.explanation: Any carbonyl compound (ketone, aldehyde, carboxylic acid, ester, amide).

free_response.prompt: As the extent of conjugation in a molecule increases, does its wavelength of maximum UV-Vis absorption shift to longer or shorter wavelengths? Answer in one word.
free_response.model_answer: Longer. More conjugation lowers the HOMO–LUMO energy gap, so a lower-energy (longer-wavelength) photon is absorbed — a red shift.
free_response.explanation: Extended conjugation delocalizes π electrons and narrows the electronic gap, which is why highly conjugated molecules (e.g., β-carotene) are colored.

source.name: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, Ch. 14: Conjugated Compounds — UV Spectroscopy

subquestions.stem: Absorbing a UV-Vis photon promotes an electron across which energy gap?
subquestions.explanation: The electron jumps from the HOMO to the LUMO.

subquestions.stem: More conjugation makes the HOMO–LUMO gap larger or smaller?
subquestions.explanation: Extended conjugation lowers (narrows) the gap.

subquestions.stem: A smaller energy gap means absorption at longer or shorter wavelength?
subquestions.explanation: Lower energy → longer wavelength (E = hc/λ).

free_response.prompt: How many neutrons are in an atom of carbon-14 (¹⁴C)? Give the number.
free_response.explanation: Carbon's atomic number (protons) is 6; the isotope label 14 is the mass number (protons + neutrons).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 2: Atoms, Molecules, and Ions

subquestions.stem: What is the atomic number (number of protons) of carbon?
subquestions.explanation: Carbon is element 6.

subquestions.stem: How do you get the neutron count from mass number A and atomic number Z?
subquestions.explanation: Neutrons = A − Z.

subquestions.stem: Compute 14 − 6.
subquestions.explanation: = 8 neutrons.

free_response.prompt: Write the ground-state electron configuration of an oxygen atom (Z = 8).
free_response.explanation: Electrons fill in order of increasing energy (1s, 2s, 2p...); oxygen's 8 electrons fill through 2p⁴.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 6: Electronic Structure and Periodic Properties

subquestions.stem: How many electrons does a neutral oxygen atom have?
subquestions.explanation: Neutral O has Z = 8 electrons.

subquestions.stem: List the subshells filled in order for the first 8 electrons.
subquestions.explanation: Fill 1s, then 2s, then 2p.

subquestions.stem: Distribute 8 electrons across 1s, 2s, 2p.

free_response.prompt: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy the n = 2 shell? Give the number.
free_response.explanation: The n = 2 shell contains one 2s and three 2p orbitals (4 orbitals × 2 electrons = 8).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 6: Electronic Structure and Periodic Properties

subquestions.stem: What formula gives the maximum electrons in a shell of principal quantum number n?
subquestions.explanation: Maximum electrons = 2n².

subquestions.stem: How many orbitals are in the n = 2 shell?
subquestions.explanation: One 2s + three 2p = 4 orbitals.

subquestions.stem: Evaluate 2n² for n = 2.

free_response.prompt: What is the energy of a photon with wavelength 500 nm? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Give the value with units.
free_response.explanation: Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength; visible-light photons carry a few ×10⁻¹⁹ J each.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 29: Introduction to Quantum Physics

subquestions.stem: Write the equation for the energy of a photon from its wavelength.
subquestions.explanation: E = hc/λ.

subquestions.stem: Convert 500 nm to meters.

free_response.prompt: In the photoelectric effect, if a photon's energy is less than the metal's work function, are any electrons ejected? Answer yes or no.
free_response.model_answer: No. An electron is ejected only if hf ≥ Φ (the work function); below that threshold no electrons are emitted, regardless of intensity.
free_response.explanation: The photoelectric effect shows light is quantized: a single photon must carry enough energy to free an electron; more low-energy photons cannot substitute.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 29: Introduction to Quantum Physics — Photon Energies

subquestions.stem: Write the photoelectric equation for the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron.
subquestions.explanation: KE_max = hf − Φ.

subquestions.stem: For an electron to escape, hf must be at least as large as what quantity?
subquestions.explanation: hf must be ≥ the work function Φ.

subquestions.stem: If hf < Φ, how many electrons are ejected?
subquestions.explanation: None — the threshold isn't met.

free_response.prompt: Moving left to right across a period, does atomic radius increase or decrease? Answer in one word.
free_response.model_answer: Decreases. Across a period the nuclear charge (Z_eff) rises while electrons enter the same shell, pulling them in tighter.
free_response.explanation: Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group (electrons occupy higher shells).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 6: Electronic Structure and Periodic Properties — Periodic Trends

subquestions.stem: Moving right across a period, how does the effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) change?
subquestions.explanation: Z_eff increases as protons are added without adding a shell.

subquestions.stem: Are the added electrons entering a new shell or the same shell across a period?
subquestions.explanation: They fill the same principal shell.

subquestions.stem: Stronger pull on the same shell makes the radius do what?
subquestions.explanation: The radius shrinks.

free_response.prompt: Going down a group in the periodic table, does the first ionization energy increase or decrease? Answer in one word.
free_response.model_answer: Decreases. Down a group the outermost electron sits in a higher shell, farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is easier to remove.
free_response.explanation: Ionization energy increases across a period and decreases down a group — opposite to atomic radius.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 6: Electronic Structure — Ionization Energy

subquestions.stem: Down a group, is the valence electron closer to or farther from the nucleus?
subquestions.explanation: It occupies a higher shell, farther from the nucleus.

subquestions.stem: Does shielding by inner electrons increase or decrease down a group?
subquestions.explanation: More inner shells mean more shielding.

subquestions.stem: Farther, more-shielded electrons are easier or harder to remove?
subquestions.explanation: Easier — so ionization energy decreases.

free_response.prompt: Which element has the highest electronegativity? Give the element name or symbol.
free_response.model_answer: Fluorine. Electronegativity increases up and to the right; excluding the noble gases, fluorine (top-right) is the most electronegative element.
free_response.explanation: The Pauling scale assigns fluorine the highest value (≈4.0); it most strongly attracts bonding electrons.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 7: Chemical Bonding — Electronegativity

subquestions.stem: In which two directions does electronegativity increase on the periodic table?
subquestions.explanation: Electronegativity rises up a group and across a period to the right.

subquestions.stem: Which group is excluded from the electronegativity trend?
subquestions.explanation: Noble gases are typically excluded (they rarely bond).

subquestions.stem: Name the top-right main-group element (excluding noble gases).
subquestions.explanation: Fluorine.

free_response.prompt: When a nucleus undergoes alpha decay, by how much does its mass number decrease? Give the number.
free_response.model_answer: An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons), so the mass number decreases by 4 (and the atomic number by 2).
free_response.explanation: Alpha decay reduces A by 4 and Z by 2; beta-minus decay leaves A unchanged but raises Z by 1.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 31: Radioactivity and Nuclear Physics

subquestions.stem: An alpha particle is the nucleus of which element?
subquestions.explanation: An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus.

subquestions.stem: How many nucleons (protons + neutrons) does an alpha particle contain?
subquestions.explanation: 2 protons + 2 neutrons = 4 nucleons.

subquestions.stem: So the parent's mass number decreases by how much?
subquestions.explanation: Mass number drops by 4.

free_response.prompt: An isotope has a half-life of 5 years. Starting with 80 g, how much remains after 15 years? Give the value with units.
free_response.explanation: Each half-life halves the amount; after n half-lives a fraction (½)ⁿ remains.

source.name: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Ch. 31: Radioactivity and Nuclear Physics — Half-Life

subquestions.stem: How many half-lives are in 15 years if each half-life is 5 years?
subquestions.explanation: 15/5 = 3 half-lives.

subquestions.stem: What fraction of the original remains after 3 half-lives?
Compute 80 g × 1/8 (give g).

free_response.prompt: How many atoms are in 2.0 mol of a substance? Use N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Give the value.
free_response.explanation: Avogadro's number links moles to particle counts; the count is a pure number (dimensionless).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 3: Composition of Substances and Solutions — The Mole

subquestions.stem: What is Avogadro's number (particles per mole)?
subquestions.explanation: N_A ≈ 6.022×10²³ mol⁻¹.

subquestions.stem: Write the relationship between number of particles N, moles n, and N_A.
subquestions.explanation: N = n × N_A.

free_response.prompt: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, you start with 1.0 mol N₂ and 1.0 mol H₂. Which reactant is the limiting reagent? Give its formula.
free_response.model_answer: The reaction needs 3 mol H₂ per mol N₂. With only 1.0 mol H₂ (which would react with just 0.33 mol N₂), H₂ runs out first, so H₂ is limiting.
free_response.explanation: The limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product given the stoichiometric ratio.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 4: Stoichiometry of Chemical Reactions — Limiting Reactant

subquestions.stem: What is the mole ratio of H₂ to N₂ in the balanced equation?
subquestions.explanation: 3 mol H₂ per 1 mol N₂.

subquestions.stem: To fully react 1.0 mol N₂, how many mol H₂ are required?
subquestions.explanation: 1.0 mol N₂ × 3 = 3.0 mol H₂ needed.

subquestions.stem: With only 1.0 mol H₂ available, which reactant is limiting?
subquestions.explanation: H₂ (there isn't enough of it).

free_response.prompt: What is the pH of a 0.010 M solution of HCl (a strong acid)? Give the numeric pH.
free_response.model_answer: HCl fully dissociates, so [H⁺] = 0.010 M. pH = −log(0.010) = 2.0.
free_response.explanation: For a strong monoprotic acid, [H⁺] equals the acid concentration; pH is its negative base-10 log.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 14: Acid-Base Equilibria — pH and pOH

subquestions.stem: A strong acid like HCl dissociates to what extent in water?
subquestions.explanation: Strong acids dissociate essentially 100%.

subquestions.stem: What is [H⁺] in 0.010 M HCl?
subquestions.explanation: [H⁺] = 0.010 M (equal to the acid concentration).

subquestions.stem: Compute pH = −log(0.010).

free_response.prompt: At 25°C, a solution has pH = 3. What is its pOH? Give the numeric value.
free_response.explanation: This follows from Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 14: Acid-Base Equilibria — pH and pOH

subquestions.stem: At 25°C, what do pH and pOH sum to?
subquestions.explanation: pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C.

subquestions.stem: Rearrange to solve for pOH given pH.
subquestions.explanation: pOH = 14 − pH.

subquestions.stem: Compute 14 − 3.

free_response.prompt: In one phrase, what distinguishes a strong acid from a weak acid in water?
free_response.model_answer: A strong acid dissociates (ionizes) essentially completely in water, whereas a weak acid ionizes only partially and establishes an equilibrium.
free_response.explanation: Strength refers to the degree of ionization, not concentration; a dilute strong acid is still 'strong.'

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 14: Acid-Base Equilibria — Strong and Weak Acids

subquestions.stem: What ion do acids donate/produce in water?
subquestions.explanation: Acids donate H⁺ (forming hydronium, H₃O⁺).

subquestions.stem: Roughly what fraction of a STRONG acid ionizes in water?
subquestions.explanation: Strong acids ionize ~completely.

subquestions.stem: A WEAK acid ionizes to what extent?
subquestions.explanation: Weak acids ionize only partially (equilibrium).

free_response.prompt: What is the conjugate base of water (H₂O)? Give the formula or name.
free_response.model_answer: Removing one H⁺ from H₂O gives OH⁻ (hydroxide), its conjugate base.
free_response.explanation: A conjugate base is what remains after an acid donates a proton; a conjugate acid is a base plus a proton.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 14: Acid-Base Equilibria — Brønsted-Lowry

subquestions.stem: To form a conjugate base, you remove which species from the acid?
subquestions.explanation: Remove one H⁺ (proton).

subquestions.stem: Take H₂O and remove one H⁺. What is left?
subquestions.explanation: H₂O − H⁺ = OH⁻.

subquestions.stem: What is the conjugate ACID of water (add H⁺)?
subquestions.explanation: H₂O + H⁺ = H₃O⁺ (hydronium).

free_response.prompt: In a buffer where the weak acid and its conjugate base are at equal concentrations, the pH equals what quantity?
free_response.model_answer: By Henderson–Hasselbalch, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). When [A⁻] = [HA], the log term is 0, so pH = pKa.
free_response.explanation: A buffer resists pH change and is most effective when pH ≈ pKa (equal acid/base forms).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 14: Acid-Base Equilibria — Buffers

subquestions.stem: Write the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.
subquestions.explanation: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

subquestions.stem: If [A⁻] = [HA], what is log([A⁻]/[HA])?
So the pH equals what?
subquestions.explanation: pH = pKa.

free_response.prompt: At the equivalence point of a strong acid–strong base titration, what is the pH (at 25°C)? Give the numeric value.
free_response.model_answer: The neutralization produces a neutral salt and water, so at the equivalence point pH = 7.
free_response.explanation: This holds only for strong–strong titrations; weak-acid titrations have an equivalence pH above 7.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 14: Acid-Base Equilibria — Titrations

subquestions.stem: At the equivalence point, how do moles of acid and base compare?
subquestions.explanation: Moles of added base equal moles of acid.

subquestions.stem: A strong acid + strong base react to form water and what kind of salt?
subquestions.explanation: A neutral (non-hydrolyzing) salt.

subquestions.stem: What pH does a neutral salt solution have at 25°C?
subquestions.explanation: pH = 7.

free_response.prompt: AgCl has Ksp = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is its molar solubility in pure water? Give the value with units.
free_response.model_answer: AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, so Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = s². Thus s = √Ksp = √(1.0×10⁻¹⁰) = 1.0×10⁻⁵ M.
free_response.explanation: For a 1:1 salt, molar solubility is the square root of Ksp.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 15: Equilibria of Other Reaction Classes — Ksp

subquestions.stem: Write the Ksp expression for AgCl dissolving into Ag⁺ and Cl⁻.
subquestions.explanation: Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻].

subquestions.stem: If solubility is s, express Ksp in terms of s for this 1:1 salt.
subquestions.explanation: [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = s, so Ksp = s².

subquestions.stem: Solve s = √(1.0×10⁻¹⁰) (give M).

free_response.prompt: Which intermolecular force is responsible for water's unusually high boiling point and surface tension? Name it.
free_response.model_answer: Hydrogen bonding. Each water molecule's polar O–H can hydrogen-bond to lone pairs on neighboring oxygens, giving water anomalously strong intermolecular attraction.
free_response.explanation: Hydrogen bonds also explain ice being less dense than liquid water and water's high specific heat.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 10: Liquids and Solids — Intermolecular Forces

subquestions.stem: Is the O–H bond in water polar or nonpolar?
subquestions.explanation: O is much more electronegative than H, so O–H is polar.

subquestions.stem: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to which highly electronegative atoms?
subquestions.explanation: H must be bonded to N, O, or F.

subquestions.stem: Name the resulting strong dipole–dipole interaction between water molecules.
subquestions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding.

free_response.prompt: What is the value of the ion-product constant of water, Kw, at 25°C? Give the value.
free_response.explanation: In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0×10⁻⁷ M, whose product is Kw = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 14: Acid-Base Equilibria — Autoionization of Water

subquestions.stem: Write the autoionization equilibrium of water.
subquestions.explanation: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.

subquestions.stem: Write Kw in terms of ion concentrations.
What is [H⁺] in pure water at 25°C?

free_response.prompt: By the Lewis definition, an acid is a species that does what with an electron pair?
free_response.model_answer: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor (a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor).
free_response.explanation: The Lewis model generalizes acidity beyond protons — e.g., BF₃ and metal cations are Lewis acids.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 15: Equilibria — Lewis Acids and Bases

subquestions.stem: What chemical entity does the Lewis model focus on (rather than H⁺)?
subquestions.explanation: Lewis theory is defined in terms of electron pairs.

subquestions.stem: A Lewis BASE does what with its electron pair?
subquestions.explanation: A Lewis base donates an electron pair.

subquestions.stem: Therefore a Lewis ACID does what with an electron pair?
subquestions.explanation: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair.

free_response.prompt: How many moles of solute are in 2.0 L of a 0.50 M solution? Give the value with units.
free_response.explanation: Molarity is moles per liter; multiplying by volume in liters gives moles.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 3: Composition of Substances and Solutions — Molarity

subquestions.stem: Define molarity in terms of moles and volume.
subquestions.explanation: Molarity = moles of solute per liter of solution.

subquestions.stem: Rearrange M = n/V to solve for moles n.
subquestions.explanation: n = M × V.

subquestions.stem: Compute (0.50 mol/L)(2.0 L) (give mol).

free_response.prompt: What type of chemical bond typically forms between a metal and a nonmetal (large electronegativity difference)? Name it.
free_response.model_answer: An ionic bond — the metal transfers electron(s) to the nonmetal, forming cations and anions held by electrostatic attraction.
free_response.explanation: Large electronegativity differences favor electron transfer (ionic); small differences favor sharing (covalent).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 7: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Geometry

subquestions.stem: In a metal + nonmetal pairing, does the metal gain or lose electrons?
subquestions.explanation: Metals lose electrons to become cations.

subquestions.stem: What are the two oppositely charged species produced called?
subquestions.explanation: A cation (metal) and an anion (nonmetal).

subquestions.stem: Electrostatic attraction between these ions is which bond type?
subquestions.explanation: Ionic bonding.

free_response.prompt: How many total valence electrons must a Lewis structure of CO₂ account for? Give the number.
free_response.model_answer: Carbon contributes 4 and each oxygen 6: 4 + 2(6) = 16 valence electrons.
free_response.explanation: Counting total valence electrons is the first step in drawing a correct Lewis structure.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 7: Chemical Bonding — Lewis Symbols and Structures

subquestions.stem: How many valence electrons does a carbon atom have?
subquestions.explanation: Carbon is in group 14: 4 valence electrons.

subquestions.stem: How many valence electrons does each oxygen atom have?
subquestions.explanation: Oxygen is in group 16: 6 valence electrons.

subquestions.stem: Total up 4 + 2(6).

free_response.prompt: What is the molecular geometry of methane, CH₄ (four bonding pairs, no lone pairs on carbon)? Name the shape.
free_response.model_answer: Four bonding domains and no lone pairs give a tetrahedral geometry with bond angles of 109.5°.
free_response.explanation: VSEPR: electron domains arrange to minimize repulsion; four equivalent domains point to the corners of a tetrahedron.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 7: Chemical Bonding — Molecular Structure (VSEPR)

subquestions.stem: How many electron domains surround the carbon in CH₄?
subquestions.explanation: Four bonding pairs = 4 domains.

subquestions.stem: With 4 domains and no lone pairs, what is the shape?
subquestions.explanation: Tetrahedral.

subquestions.stem: What is the ideal bond angle in a tetrahedral molecule?

free_response.prompt: What is the molecular geometry of water, H₂O (two bonding pairs and two lone pairs on oxygen)? Name the shape.
free_response.model_answer: The oxygen has four electron domains (tetrahedral electron geometry), but with two lone pairs the atoms form a bent (angular) shape (~104.5°).
free_response.explanation: Molecular geometry describes only atom positions; lone pairs occupy space and bend the H–O–H angle.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 7: Chemical Bonding — Molecular Structure (VSEPR)

subquestions.stem: Count the electron domains around oxygen in water (bonds + lone pairs).
subquestions.explanation: 2 bonding + 2 lone pairs = 4 domains.

subquestions.stem: What is the electron-domain geometry for 4 domains?
subquestions.explanation: Tetrahedral electron geometry.

subquestions.stem: Ignoring the two lone pairs, what shape do the three atoms make?
subquestions.explanation: Bent (angular).

free_response.prompt: What is the hybridization of a carbon atom bonded to four other atoms with only single bonds (e.g., in CH₄)? Give the hybridization.
free_response.model_answer: Four regions of electron density require four equivalent hybrid orbitals: sp³.
free_response.explanation: The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of electron domains: 2→sp, 3→sp², 4→sp³.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 8: Advanced Theories of Covalent Bonding — Hybridization

subquestions.stem: How many regions of electron density surround this carbon?
subquestions.explanation: Four single bonds = 4 regions.

subquestions.stem: How many atomic orbitals must mix to make 4 hybrids (one s and how many p)?
subquestions.explanation: One s + three p orbitals.

subquestions.stem: Name the resulting hybridization.
subquestions.explanation: sp³.

free_response.prompt: Is carbon dioxide (CO₂) a polar or nonpolar molecule? Answer polar or nonpolar.
free_response.model_answer: Nonpolar. CO₂ is linear and symmetric, so its two equal C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
free_response.explanation: A molecule can have polar bonds yet be nonpolar overall if its geometry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 7: Chemical Bonding — Molecular Polarity

subquestions.stem: Are the individual C=O bonds polar? (yes/no)
subquestions.explanation: Yes — O is more electronegative than C, so each C=O is polar.

subquestions.stem: What is the shape of the CO₂ molecule?
subquestions.explanation: Linear (O=C=O, 180°).

subquestions.stem: In a symmetric linear molecule, do the opposing bond dipoles add or cancel?
subquestions.explanation: They cancel, giving a nonpolar molecule.

free_response.prompt: A carbon–carbon double bond (C=C) consists of how many sigma and how many pi bonds?
free_response.model_answer: A double bond is one sigma (σ) bond plus one pi (π) bond.
free_response.explanation: The first bond between two atoms is always a sigma bond; each additional bond in a multiple bond is a pi bond (so a triple bond = 1σ + 2π).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 8: Advanced Theories of Covalent Bonding — Sigma and Pi Bonds

subquestions.stem: What kind of bond is the single (first) bond between two atoms?
subquestions.explanation: The first bond is always a sigma (σ) bond.

subquestions.stem: Any additional bonds in a multiple bond are what type?
subquestions.explanation: Additional bonds are pi (π) bonds.

subquestions.stem: So a C=C double bond contains how many of each?
subquestions.explanation: 1 sigma + 1 pi.

free_response.prompt: Of London dispersion forces, dipole–dipole forces, and hydrogen bonding, which is the strongest? Name it.
free_response.model_answer: Hydrogen bonding is the strongest of these three intermolecular forces.
free_response.explanation: Typical ordering (weakest to strongest): London dispersion < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding (a specially strong dipole–dipole interaction).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 10: Liquids and Solids — Intermolecular Forces

subquestions.stem: Which of the three is the weakest, present in all molecules?
subquestions.explanation: London dispersion forces (present in all molecules).

subquestions.stem: Hydrogen bonding is a specially strong form of which interaction?
subquestions.explanation: It is a strong dipole–dipole interaction.

subquestions.stem: So which of the three is strongest?
subquestions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding.

free_response.prompt: Between methane (CH₄) and water (H₂O), which has the higher boiling point? Give the substance.
free_response.model_answer: Water. It forms hydrogen bonds, a much stronger intermolecular force than the London dispersion forces in nonpolar methane, so more energy is needed to vaporize it.
free_response.explanation: Boiling point tracks intermolecular force strength: stronger IMFs → higher boiling point.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 10: Liquids and Solids — Intermolecular Forces

subquestions.stem: What is the only intermolecular force available to nonpolar CH₄?
subquestions.explanation: Only London dispersion forces.

subquestions.stem: What stronger intermolecular force does water have?
subquestions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding.

subquestions.stem: Stronger intermolecular forces give a higher or lower boiling point?
subquestions.explanation: Higher — so water boils at a much higher temperature.

free_response.prompt: What is the formal charge on the nitrogen atom in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺? Give the value with sign.
free_response.model_answer: FC = (valence e⁻) − (nonbonding e⁻) − ½(bonding e⁻) = 5 − 0 − ½(8) = 5 − 4 = +1.
free_response.explanation: Formal charge helps choose the best Lewis structure; summed formal charges equal the ion's overall charge.

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 7: Chemical Bonding — Formal Charges

subquestions.stem: Write the formula for formal charge.
subquestions.explanation: FC = (valence) − (nonbonding e⁻) − ½(bonding e⁻).

subquestions.stem: For N in NH₄⁺: valence = 5, nonbonding = 0, bonding electrons = 8. Plug in.
Evaluate 5 − 4.

free_response.prompt: What term describes the situation where a molecule's true bonding is a blend (average) of two or more valid Lewis structures? Give the term.
free_response.model_answer: Resonance. The actual molecule is a resonance hybrid — an average of the contributing Lewis structures, with delocalized electrons.
free_response.explanation: Resonance delocalizes electrons and stabilizes molecules/ions (e.g., benzene, carbonate, the carboxylate anion).

source.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Ch. 7: Chemical Bonding — Resonance

subquestions.stem: If one Lewis structure can't fully describe the bonding, what do you draw instead?
subquestions.explanation: Draw two or more valid Lewis (resonance) structures.

subquestions.stem: The real molecule is an average of these, called a resonance ____.
subquestions.explanation: A resonance hybrid.

subquestions.stem: What is the single term for this phenomenon?
subquestions.explanation: Resonance.

free_response.prompt: Liquid–liquid extraction separates compounds based on differences in which property between two immiscible solvents? Name it.
free_response.model_answer: Solubility. A solute partitions between two immiscible solvents according to its relative solubility (the partition/distribution coefficient).
free_response.explanation: "Like dissolves like": a compound concentrates in the solvent it is more soluble in, allowing separation.

source.name: LibreTexts Chemistry — Liquid-Liquid Extraction

subquestions.stem: An extraction uses two solvents that do NOT mix, described as what?
subquestions.explanation: Two immiscible solvents (e.g., water and diethyl ether).

subquestions.stem: A solute distributes between the two layers according to its relative what?
subquestions.explanation: Its relative solubility.

subquestions.stem: The ratio of concentrations in the two solvents is called the ____ coefficient.
subquestions.explanation: The partition (distribution) coefficient.

free_response.prompt: In an acid–base extraction, adding aqueous NaOH deprotonates a carboxylic acid (RCOOH) to give what water-soluble species? Name it.
free_response.model_answer: The carboxylate ion (RCOO⁻). Deprotonation makes the molecule ionic, so it moves from the organic layer into the aqueous layer.
free_response.explanation: Acid–base extraction exploits how (de)protonation switches a compound between neutral (organic-soluble) and ionic (water-soluble) forms.

source.name: LibreTexts Chemistry — Acid-Base Extraction

subquestions.stem: Is neutral RCOOH more soluble in the organic layer or the water layer?
subquestions.explanation: Neutral organic acids favor the organic layer.

subquestions.stem: What does NaOH remove from RCOOH?
subquestions.explanation: NaOH removes a proton (H⁺).

subquestions.stem: Name the resulting anion.
subquestions.explanation: The carboxylate ion, RCOO⁻, which dissolves in water.

free_response.prompt: Distillation separates a mixture of liquids based on differences in which physical property? Name it.
free_response.model_answer: Boiling point (volatility). The component with the lower boiling point vaporizes preferentially, then is condensed and collected.
free_response.explanation: Fractional distillation is used when boiling points are close; simple distillation suffices when they differ widely.

source.name: LibreTexts Chemistry — Distillation

subquestions.stem: Which component vaporizes first when the mixture is heated?
subquestions.explanation: The component with the lower boiling point (more volatile).

subquestions.stem: After vaporizing, the vapor is cooled and turned back to liquid in which step?
subquestions.explanation: Condensation (in the condenser).
