subquestions.explanation: Intrinsic motivation is undermined - the hallmark of overjustification.

subquestions.stem: This is called the ___ effect.
subquestions.explanation: Over-justifying the behavior with an external reward crowds out intrinsic interest.

questions.stem: The framework contrasting motivation 'from within the person' with motivation 'driven by external consequences' is:
questions.explanation: Doing something for its own enjoyment is intrinsic motivation; doing it for a reward or to avoid punishment is extrinsic motivation. Drive-reduction concerns reducing biological needs, Yerkes-Dodson relates arousal to performance, and incentive salience is a neuroscience concept about reward 'wanting.'

subquestions.stem: Doing something for its own enjoyment is ___ motivation.
subquestions.explanation: Intrinsic motivation comes from internal satisfaction.

subquestions.stem: Doing something to gain a reward or avoid punishment is ___ motivation.
subquestions.explanation: Extrinsic motivation is driven by external consequences.

questions.stem: That the effort-framing benefit was largest among highly conscientious participants draws on which approach to personality?
questions.explanation: Conscientiousness is one of the Big Five (OCEAN) traits, stable dimensions on which people differ - the trait approach. The psychoanalytic approach emphasizes unconscious conflict, the humanistic approach emphasizes self-actualization, and the behaviorist approach emphasizes learning histories rather than trait dimensions.

subquestions.stem: Conscientiousness (organized, persistent, disciplined) is one of the:
subquestions.explanation: Conscientiousness is a Big Five dimension.

subquestions.stem: Trait theories describe personality as:
options: stable dimensions on which people differ
subquestions.explanation: Traits are enduring dimensions used to describe and predict behavior.

questions.subtopic: Beliefs about ability and achievement motivation
questions.stem: That difficulty increased persistence in the 'effort' framing but not the 'intelligence' framing relates most to which idea?
options: Beliefs about the causes of success shape motivation (mindset)
questions.explanation: Whether people attribute success to malleable effort/strategy or to fixed ability shapes how they respond to difficulty; an effort belief sustains persistence after setbacks. Drive reduction concerns biological needs, the refractory period is a neuronal property, and mere exposure is about familiarity increasing liking.

subquestions.stem: The two groups differed in what they believed drives success: fixed intelligence vs. ___.
subquestions.explanation: The contrast was a fixed-ability belief vs. an effort/strategy belief.

subquestions.stem: Believing effort drives success tends to ___ persistence after failure.
subquestions.explanation: An effort belief frames setbacks as surmountable, sustaining persistence.

passages.passage:
Researchers ran three studies of behavior in groups. In Study 1, a participant judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line, answering aloud after several confederates. On critical trials the confederates unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer. Participants conformed to the wrong answer on about 35% of critical trials, and three-quarters conformed at least once; conformity fell sharply when a single confederate broke from the majority. Most conformers later said they knew the group was wrong but did not want to stand out.

In Study 2, participants completed either a simple, well-practiced task or a complex, unfamiliar task, alone or in front of an audience. An audience improved performance on the simple task but worsened it on the complex task.

In Study 3, participants heard what sounded like a fellow participant having a medical emergency in another room. When participants believed they were the only witness, 85% sought help within a minute; when they believed four others were also present, only 31% did, and those who helped took longer. Interviews suggested that the presence of others reduced each individual's felt responsibility.

The authors distinguished going along with a group to fit in from the effect of an audience on task performance, and linked Study 3 to a well-documented reduction in helping as the number of bystanders rises. They emphasized that these effects reflect the social situation rather than stable personality differences among the participants.

passage_source.name: OpenStax Psychology 2e (Ch. 12, Social Psychology)

questions.stem: Participants in Study 1 conforming despite privately knowing the answer was wrong best reflects:
questions.explanation: Normative social influence is conforming to gain acceptance or avoid standing out, which is exactly what conformers described. Informational influence is conforming because you believe the group is more accurate; obedience involves orders from an authority; and group polarization is discussion making views more extreme.

subquestions.stem: Conformers said they knew the group was wrong but did not want to stand out. Were they seeking correct information or social acceptance?
subquestions.explanation: Their motive was fitting in, not getting the answer right.

subquestions.stem: Conforming to gain acceptance / avoid disapproval is ___ social influence.
subquestions.explanation: Normative influence is about social approval.

subquestions.stem: Conforming because you think the group knows better (for accuracy) would instead be ___.
subquestions.explanation: Seeking accuracy from others is informational influence.

questions.stem: Conformity 'fell sharply when a single confederate broke from the majority.' This shows conformity depends strongly on:
options: The difficulty of the perceptual task
The size of the monetary reward
questions.explanation: Losing unanimity - even one dissenter - dramatically reduces conformity, the key manipulation here. The perceptual task was easy and unchanged, no reward was involved, and the passage attributes the drop to the broken consensus, not to self-esteem.

subquestions.stem: What changed when one confederate dissented?
options: The group was no longer unanimous
subquestions.explanation: A single dissenter breaks the group's unanimity.

subquestions.stem: A single ally / loss of unanimity ___ conformity.
subquestions.explanation: Breaking unanimity sharply reduces conformity pressure.

questions.stem: Study 2's pattern - an audience helps simple tasks but hurts complex ones - is the classic finding of:
questions.explanation: Social facilitation: the presence of others boosts performance on simple/well-learned tasks (the dominant response) but impairs it on complex/novel tasks. Social loafing is reduced individual effort in groups, deindividuation is loss of self-awareness in crowds, and groupthink is flawed group decision-making.

subquestions.stem: The audience improved which task and worsened which?
subquestions.explanation: Arousal from an audience aids dominant (well-learned) responses and hurts novel ones.

subquestions.stem: This audience effect on performance is called:
subquestions.explanation: The performance-modulating presence of others is social facilitation.

questions.stem: The drop from 85% to 31% helping as more witnesses were believed present illustrates:
options: Social loafing on a shared physical task
The bystander effect via diffusion of responsibility
questions.explanation: The bystander effect is reduced helping as group size grows, driven here by diffusion of responsibility (each person feels less personally responsible). Social loafing concerns effort on a joint task, informational influence is about accuracy, and inclusive fitness concerns helping genetic relatives - none of which the interviews indicated.

subquestions.stem: As the number of believed witnesses rose, helping:
subquestions.explanation: Helping dropped from 85% (alone) to 31% (with others believed present).

subquestions.stem: Each person feeling less personally responsible when others are present is called:
subquestions.explanation: Responsibility is spread across bystanders, so each feels less of it.

subquestions.stem: This reduction in helping as bystanders increase is the ___ effect.
subquestions.explanation: It is the bystander effect.

questions.stem: The authors' emphasis that these effects 'reflect the social situation rather than stable personality differences' aligns with which broad claim of social psychology?
options: Behavior is determined mainly by fixed traits
Situations exert powerful influence on behavior
The fundamental attribution error is always accurate
questions.explanation: A central lesson of social psychology is the power of the situation to shape behavior, which these three studies illustrate. The trait-only and genetic-determinism options contradict the authors' point, and the fundamental attribution error is precisely the mistake (over-attributing to disposition) these results warn against.

subquestions.stem: Did the studies attribute behavior to who the people were, or to the situation?
subquestions.explanation: The effects came from situational structure, not personality.

subquestions.stem: Over-attributing others' behavior to personality while ignoring the situation is the ___ (which these results caution against).
subquestions.explanation: The fundamental attribution error underweights situational causes.

passages.passage:
A study examined how persuasive messages change attitudes. Undergraduates read an editorial advocating a new campus exam policy. The message was either strong (well-reasoned arguments) or weak (superficial slogans), and was attributed either to a distinguished professor or to a first-year student. Crucially, half the participants were told the policy would take effect next year (high personal relevance) and half were told it would begin in a decade (low relevance).

Among high-relevance readers, attitude change depended almost entirely on argument strength and hardly at all on the source; among low-relevance readers, the reverse held - the prestigious source mattered, but argument quality did not. A follow-up a week later showed that attitudes formed by high-relevance readers persisted and better predicted sign-up behavior than those of low-relevance readers.

In a second study, participants who volunteered to argue publicly for a position they privately opposed later shifted their private attitudes toward that position - but only when they felt they had freely chosen to do so and were paid little. Those paid a large sum, or who felt coerced, showed no attitude change.

The authors mapped the first study onto a dual-route model of persuasion: one route processes the substance of a message when motivation is high, while the other relies on surface cues when motivation is low. They explained the second study as the reduction of an uncomfortable inconsistency between behavior and belief, resolved by changing the belief when the behavior could not be justified by an external incentive.

passage_source.name: OpenStax Psychology 2e (Ch. 12, Social Psychology)

questions.stem: High-relevance readers' reliance on argument strength reflects which route of the elaboration likelihood model?
questions.explanation: In the elaboration likelihood model, motivated (here, high-relevance) recipients take the central route, effortfully evaluating argument quality. The peripheral route relies on surface cues such as source prestige. Classical conditioning and mere exposure are different attitude-formation mechanisms.

subquestions.stem: High-relevance readers were persuaded by what?
subquestions.explanation: They responded to argument strength, not the source.

subquestions.stem: Effortful processing of a message's substance is the ___ route.
subquestions.explanation: The central route involves high elaboration on content.

questions.stem: Low-relevance readers being swayed by the source's prestige rather than argument quality exemplifies:
questions.explanation: Unmotivated recipients take the peripheral route, leaning on surface cues like who delivered the message. The central route would attend to argument quality; cognitive dissonance and foot-in-the-door are separate phenomena not at issue here.

subquestions.stem: Low-relevance readers relied on a surface cue - who said it. Is that deep or shallow processing?
subquestions.explanation: Using source cues instead of content is shallow processing.

subquestions.stem: Relying on surface cues (source, attractiveness) is the ___ route.
subquestions.explanation: Peripheral processing uses heuristic cues.

questions.stem: That high-relevance (central-route) attitudes persisted longer and better predicted behavior supports which generalization?
options: Central-route attitude change is more durable and predictive of behavior
Source cues create the most lasting change
questions.explanation: Central-route change, built on effortful processing, is generally more durable, resistant to counter-persuasion, and predictive of behavior - matching the week-later sign-up data. The other options contradict the findings or overstate the role of peripheral cues.

subquestions.stem: Which readers' attitudes better predicted later sign-up?
subquestions.explanation: Central-route attitudes better predicted behavior.

subquestions.stem: Central-route change tends to be ___ than peripheral-route change.
subquestions.explanation: Effortful, content-based change is more enduring.

questions.stem: Study 2's result - attitude shift only with free choice and small pay - is the signature of:
options: Cognitive dissonance reduction under insufficient justification
Operant reinforcement of the essay behavior
questions.explanation: Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory predicts that freely arguing against one's beliefs for little pay creates discomfort that cannot be blamed on the reward (insufficient justification), so people change the attitude. Large pay provides sufficient external justification, eliminating dissonance. Reinforcement or obedience would not require the free-choice/low-pay pattern.

subquestions.stem: Arguing publicly against one's private belief creates an uncomfortable:
subquestions.explanation: That inconsistency is cognitive dissonance.

subquestions.stem: With little pay, the behavior cannot be blamed on money, so to reduce discomfort people change their:
subquestions.explanation: They bring the attitude in line with the behavior.

subquestions.stem: Large pay provides ___ justification, so no attitude change is needed.
subquestions.explanation: Ample external reward justifies the behavior, so dissonance is low.

passages.passage:
Researchers studied how people view themselves and explain behavior. In Study 1, community volunteers completed a scale measuring their belief that they could organize and execute the actions needed to reach specific goals. Independently, they rated how much they felt their life outcomes were controlled by their own actions versus by luck or powerful others. Volunteers high on the first measure attempted harder tasks, persisted longer after setbacks, and reported less anxiety. Those who attributed outcomes mostly to outside forces set fewer goals and gave up sooner.

In Study 2, participants read vignettes about a student who failed an exam. When explaining the student's failure, observers most often cited the student's laziness or low ability, rarely mentioning the situation (an unfair test, a family emergency). Yet when participants recalled a time they themselves had failed, they overwhelmingly cited situational causes. In a variation, participants watched a peer perform poorly under obvious time pressure; even so, most still rated the peer as low in ability.

The authors linked Study 1 to two related constructs: a person's belief in their capability to succeed at specific tasks, and a general expectancy about whether outcomes are internally or externally controlled. They interpreted Study 2 as showing a systematic bias in how observers explain others' behavior, together with a divergence between how people explain their own versus others' outcomes. They stressed that these attribution tendencies operate even when situational information is clearly available.

passage_source.name: OpenStax Psychology 2e (Ch. 11, Personality; Ch. 12, Social Psychology)

questions.stem: The first measure in Study 1 - belief in one's capability to execute the actions needed to reach goals - is:
questions.explanation: Bandura's self-efficacy is the belief in one's capability to succeed at specific tasks, which predicts effort and persistence - as observed. Self-esteem is global self-worth, locus of control is the second construct in the study, and the self-serving bias is an attribution pattern.

subquestions.stem: The measure concerned belief in one's ability to succeed at specific tasks, not overall self-worth. That is:
subquestions.explanation: Task-specific capability belief is self-efficacy.

subquestions.stem: High self-efficacy predicted what after setbacks?
subquestions.explanation: Self-efficacy supports persistence in the face of difficulty.

questions.stem: Rating how much outcomes are controlled by one's own actions versus luck or powerful others measures the construct of:
questions.explanation: Rotter's locus of control is a general expectancy about whether outcomes are internally (own actions) or externally (luck, others) controlled. Self-efficacy is task-specific capability, self-concept is one's overall self-description, and self-handicapping is creating obstacles to excuse failure.

subquestions.stem: Believing you control your outcomes is a(n) ___ locus of control.
subquestions.explanation: Internal locus attributes outcomes to one's own actions.

subquestions.stem: Believing luck or powerful others control outcomes is a(n) ___ locus of control.
subquestions.explanation: External locus attributes outcomes to outside forces.

questions.stem: Observers blaming the failing student's laziness or ability while ignoring the situation illustrates:
questions.explanation: The fundamental attribution error is over-attributing others' behavior to disposition while underweighting situational causes - seen even under obvious time pressure. The self-serving bias concerns explaining one's own outcomes, the just-world hypothesis is believing people get what they deserve, and the halo effect is one trait coloring overall judgment.

subquestions.stem: In explaining someone else's behavior, observers over-weighted which kind of cause?
subquestions.explanation: They favored personal/dispositional explanations.

subquestions.stem: Over-attributing others' behavior to disposition and underweighting the situation is the:
subquestions.explanation: That is the fundamental attribution error (correspondence bias).

questions.stem: The divergence - situational explanations for one's OWN failure but dispositional explanations for OTHERS' - is:
questions.explanation: The actor-observer bias is the tendency to attribute our own behavior to the situation but others' behavior to their dispositions - exactly the pattern across the two vignettes. The fundamental attribution error names only the observer side, the false-consensus effect is overestimating how many share our views, and self-efficacy is unrelated.

subquestions.stem: For their own failure, participants cited which causes, and for others' failure, which?
options: Situational for self; dispositional for others
Dispositional for self; situational for others
subquestions.explanation: Own failure -> situation; others' failure -> disposition.

subquestions.stem: This difference between explaining one's own versus others' behavior is the ___ bias.
subquestions.explanation: It is the actor-observer asymmetry.

questions.stem: According to George Herbert Mead, the internalized sense of the general expectations of society - which children increasingly take into account - is:
questions.explanation: Mead's 'generalized other' is the internalized attitudes and expectations of society as a whole. The 'I' is the spontaneous, unsocialized self (contrasted with the socialized 'me'); the looking-glass self is Cooley's concept; and the id is a Freudian structure.

subquestions.stem: Mead distinguished the spontaneous '___' from the socialized 'me'.
subquestions.explanation: The 'I' is the impulsive, unsocialized aspect of the self.

subquestions.stem: The internalized attitudes of the whole community form the:
subquestions.explanation: Taking the role of the generalized other reflects society's expectations.

passages.passage:
A study tested how awareness of a negative stereotype affects performance and self-presentation. Two groups of equally qualified students took the same difficult verbal test. In the 'diagnostic' condition, the test was described as measuring underlying ability; in the 'nondiagnostic' condition, it was described as a problem-solving exercise unrelated to ability. Students from a group stereotyped as weaker in the domain scored lower than others in the diagnostic condition but scored equally in the nondiagnostic condition. Merely asking students to record their group membership before a diagnostic test reproduced the gap.

In a second study, participants prepared for a mock interview. Told the interviewer valued modesty, they described themselves cautiously; told the interviewer admired confidence, the same participants emphasized their strengths. Observers who saw only one version rated the participants accordingly, and participants reported deliberately tailoring the impression they gave.

The authors interpreted the first study as evidence that the fear of confirming a negative group stereotype can itself depress performance, independent of ability, and that subtle cues activate this fear. They interpreted the second as an example of managing the impression one presents to different audiences, comparing it to an actor shifting performances between a front region and a back region. They cautioned that persistent performance gaps in real settings may partly reflect such situational threats and unequal conditions rather than fixed differences in ability between groups.

passage_source.name: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e (Ch. 12, Social Psychology)

questions.stem: The lower scores only in the 'diagnostic' condition, erased in the 'nondiagnostic' condition, best demonstrate:
options: A genuine ability difference between groups
questions.explanation: Stereotype threat is the fear of confirming a negative stereotype about one's group, which can depress performance independent of ability - hence the gap appears only when the test is framed as diagnostic of ability. A true ability difference would appear in both conditions; mere exposure and deindividuation are unrelated.

subquestions.stem: Did the stereotyped group score lower in both conditions, or only when the test was called diagnostic of ability?
subquestions.explanation: The gap appeared only under the ability-diagnostic framing.

subquestions.stem: If ability were truly lower, the gap would appear in both conditions. Its disappearance points to a ___ cause.
subquestions.explanation: A frame-dependent gap indicates a situational, not fixed, cause.

subquestions.stem: Fear of confirming a negative stereotype impairing performance is called:
subquestions.explanation: This is stereotype threat.

questions.stem: Participants tailoring their self-descriptions to what each interviewer valued exemplifies:
questions.explanation: Impression management is controlling the impression others form of us, here by adjusting self-presentation to the audience's values. Dissonance concerns internal inconsistency, the actor-observer bias concerns attribution, and social loafing concerns reduced group effort.

subquestions.stem: Participants changed how they portrayed themselves depending on the:
subquestions.explanation: They adapted to the interviewer's stated preferences.

subquestions.stem: Controlling the impression others form of you is:
subquestions.explanation: That is impression management / self-presentation.

questions.stem: The comparison to 'an actor shifting performances between a front region and a back region' refers to whose dramaturgical approach?
questions.explanation: Goffman's dramaturgical approach frames social life as theater, with front stage (performing for an audience) and back stage (relaxing out of view). Festinger (dissonance), Milgram (obedience), and Piaget (cognitive development) are associated with different ideas.

subquestions.stem: The 'front region' (front stage) is where we:
subquestions.explanation: Front stage is the performance region.

subquestions.stem: This theatrical metaphor for social life is credited to:
subquestions.explanation: Erving Goffman developed the dramaturgical approach.

questions.stem: The negative belief that a group is 'weaker in the domain' is best labeled a:
questions.explanation: A stereotype is a cognitive belief/generalization about a group. Prejudice is the affective attitude (feeling) toward a group, discrimination is the behavioral act of unequal treatment, and a norm is a shared expectation for behavior.

subquestions.stem: A generalized belief about a group's characteristics is a:
subquestions.explanation: Beliefs are the cognitive component: stereotypes.

subquestions.stem: Acting on such a belief to treat the group unfairly would be:
subquestions.explanation: Behavioral unequal treatment is discrimination.

questions.stem: The authors' caution that real-world performance gaps 'may partly reflect situational threats and unequal conditions rather than fixed differences' is most relevant to debates about:
options: Explanations of social inequality between groups
questions.explanation: Attributing group gaps to unequal conditions (structural) versus fixed ability (individual) is central to explaining social inequality. The demographic transition and population pyramid concern population change, and the sick role concerns illness behavior.

subquestions.stem: Attributing group gaps to unequal conditions is a ___ explanation; attributing them to fixed ability is a(n) ___ explanation.
subquestions.explanation: Conditions = structural; fixed ability = individual.

subquestions.stem: This debate concerns the causes of:
subquestions.explanation: It is about the origins of inequality between groups.

passages.passage:
Sociologists analyzed how a chronic illness is understood and managed in a mid-sized city. Using surveys and interviews, they documented three patterns. First, physicians and hospitals coordinated with schools and workplaces so that ill members could be temporarily excused from normal duties while being expected to seek treatment and cooperate with doctors. Second, patients with more education and income obtained diagnoses and specialist care far faster than poorer patients, who often relied on crowded clinics; the researchers traced this to differences in insurance, flexible work hours, and familiarity with medical institutions. Third, behaviors once seen as ordinary or as moral failings - such as persistent sadness or restlessness - were increasingly defined and treated as medical conditions.

The team framed each pattern with a different theoretical lens. The coordinated excusing of the sick was described as an institution maintaining social stability by managing how illness disrupts roles. The unequal access was described in terms of groups with different amounts of resources and power competing for a scarce good. The redefinition of ordinary behaviors as illnesses was described as a process by which the meaning of 'sickness' is negotiated and expanded within a society. In interviews, patients described how a formal diagnosis changed how others treated them, sometimes granting sympathy and sometimes attaching stigma. The authors noted that the fastest-growing diagnoses clustered among specific age groups, and that the city's aging population was projected to raise overall demand for chronic-disease care over the coming decades.

passage_source.name: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e (Ch. 1, An Introduction to Sociology; Ch. 19, Health and Medicine)

questions.stem: Describing medicine as 'an institution maintaining social stability by managing how illness disrupts roles' reflects which paradigm, and connects to whose 'sick role' concept?
questions.explanation: Framing an institution by how it preserves social stability is structural functionalism; Parsons's 'sick role' casts illness as a temporary sanctioned role with rights (excused duties) and obligations (seek care). Conflict theory emphasizes power struggles, symbolic interactionism emphasizes meaning, and feminist theory emphasizes gendered structures.

subquestions.stem: A view emphasizing how institutions keep society stable and functioning is:
subquestions.explanation: Functionalism focuses on stability and the functions institutions serve.

subquestions.stem: The idea that being 'sick' is a temporary social role with rights and duties (from Talcott Parsons) is the:
subquestions.explanation: Parsons described the sick role.

questions.stem: Explaining unequal access as 'groups with different resources and power competing for a scarce good' is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Conflict theory (rooted in Marx) analyzes society as competition between groups over scarce resources and power - here, unequal access to care. Functionalism stresses stability, symbolic interactionism stresses meaning in interaction, and exchange theory models individual cost-benefit decisions.

subquestions.stem: A lens focused on competition over scarce resources and power between groups is ___ theory.
subquestions.explanation: Competition over resources/power is the conflict lens.

subquestions.stem: Conflict theory traces its roots most directly to:
subquestions.explanation: Marx is the foundational figure for conflict theory.

questions.stem: Redefining ordinary behaviors as illnesses, framed as negotiating the 'meaning of sickness,' together with the finding that a diagnosis changed how others treated patients, reflects:
questions.explanation: Symbolic interactionism focuses on how meanings (like 'sick') are created and negotiated in interaction, and medicalization is the process of defining non-medical problems as medical ones. Functionalism and germ theory address different questions, and the demographic transition concerns population change.

subquestions.stem: A focus on how meanings (like 'sick') are created and negotiated in interaction is:
subquestions.explanation: Meaning-in-interaction is the symbolic-interactionist lens.

subquestions.stem: The process of defining non-medical problems as medical ones is:
subquestions.explanation: That is medicalization.

questions.stem: Which of the three lenses is a MICRO-level (rather than macro-level) approach?
questions.explanation: Symbolic interactionism analyzes small-scale, everyday interactions and meanings (micro level). Structural functionalism and conflict theory analyze large-scale social structures (macro level), so the 'all three are macro' option is incorrect.

subquestions.stem: Functionalism and conflict theory analyze society at which level?
subquestions.explanation: Both are macro-level, big-picture paradigms.

subquestions.stem: Symbolic interactionism analyzes which kind of interactions?
subquestions.explanation: It is a micro-level focus on everyday meaning-making.

questions.stem: The projection that the city's aging population will raise chronic-disease demand draws on which demographic idea?
options: Population aging shifting the age structure
A demographic dividend from high fertility
questions.explanation: An aging population means a rising share of older people, shifting the age structure toward higher chronic-disease demand. The misinformation effect and social facilitation are psychological phenomena, and a demographic dividend arises from a large working-age share, not aging.

subquestions.stem: An 'aging population' means the share of which group is rising?
subquestions.explanation: Aging shifts the distribution toward older ages.

subquestions.stem: A tool that displays a population's age-sex structure is a:
subquestions.explanation: Population pyramids show age-sex structure.

passages.passage:
A longitudinal study followed 8,000 adults for 15 years to examine links between social position and health. Participants were grouped by socioeconomic status (SES), a composite of income, education, and occupational prestige. Age-adjusted rates of chronic illness and mortality declined steadily at each higher step of the SES ladder - not merely a gap between rich and poor, but a graded relationship across the whole range. The pattern held after controlling for smoking and diet, and was partly explained by chronic stress, worse neighborhood conditions, and unequal access to preventive care.

Participants were also classified by the neighborhood where they lived. Lower-SES families were concentrated in areas with fewer clinics, more pollution, and less green space; researchers described these areas as products of long-standing residential segregation. Children raised in the lowest-SES neighborhoods were less likely to reach a higher SES than their parents, a pattern the authors linked to unequal schools and social networks.

Finally, the study noted a demographic shift: as the population aged and birth rates fell, the ratio of working-age adults to dependents changed, straining programs that fund elder care. The authors argued that health follows a social gradient, that place and inequality shape opportunity across generations, and that population structure interacts with these inequalities to shape a society's future needs. They emphasized that individual choices operated within, and were constrained by, these structural conditions.

passage_source.name: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e (Ch. 9, Social Stratification; Ch. 20, Population, Urbanization, and the Environment)

questions.stem: The 'graded relationship across the whole range,' not just a rich-poor gap, is best described as:
questions.explanation: A step-by-step improvement in health at each higher SES level is the socioeconomic (social) gradient in health. A threshold effect would show a single cutoff, not a gradient; the demographic transition concerns birth/death rates; and the sick role concerns illness behavior.

subquestions.stem: Health improved at which points of the SES ladder?
subquestions.explanation: Improvement occurred at every step, not just the extremes.

subquestions.stem: A continuous, step-by-step relationship across all levels is called a:
subquestions.explanation: That continuous pattern is a gradient.

questions.stem: In this study, SES was measured as a composite of:
questions.explanation: SES is multidimensional, typically combining income, education, and occupational prestige - the definition used here. Income alone, age/sex, or neighborhood alone each capture only part (or none) of SES.

subquestions.stem: Which is NOT one of the usual components of SES?
subquestions.explanation: Blood type is unrelated to SES.

subquestions.stem: Measuring standing along several dimensions (class, status, power) echoes which theorist?
subquestions.explanation: Weber described a multidimensional view of stratification.

questions.stem: Concentrating lower-SES families in areas with fewer resources, described as products of 'residential segregation,' is an example of:
questions.explanation: The uneven distribution of resources and environmental burdens across places is spatial inequality, and poorer neighborhoods bearing more pollution is environmental injustice. Social facilitation is a group-performance effect, the demographic transition concerns population change, and meritocracy is an ideology about earned position.

subquestions.stem: The unequal distribution of resources across places is ___ inequality.
subquestions.explanation: Inequality tied to place/geography is spatial.

subquestions.stem: Poorer neighborhoods bearing disproportionate pollution reflects environmental:
subquestions.explanation: That unequal burden is environmental injustice.

questions.stem: Children from the lowest-SES neighborhoods rarely exceeding their parents' SES illustrates:
questions.explanation: When class position persists from parents to children, mobility is low and advantages/disadvantages are reproduced across generations (social reproduction). High mobility would mean children readily change SES; a demographic dividend is a population-age concept; and universal upward mobility contradicts the data.

subquestions.stem: Moving to a different SES than one's parents is ___ mobility.
subquestions.explanation: Across generations = intergenerational mobility.

subquestions.stem: When advantages and disadvantages pass across generations, keeping the class structure stable, sociologists call it social:
subquestions.explanation: That persistence is social reproduction.

questions.stem: The shift in which an aging population and falling births change the ratio of workers to dependents concerns the:
options: dependency ratio, tied to the demographic transition
questions.explanation: The dependency ratio compares non-working (young + old) to working-age people; aging plus low fertility (late demographic transition) raises it. The other options are psychological/social-cognitive concepts unrelated to population structure.

subquestions.stem: Falling birth rates plus longer lifespans are features of the:
subquestions.explanation: These are hallmarks of the demographic transition.

subquestions.stem: The ratio of non-working (young + old) to working-age people is the ___ ratio.
subquestions.explanation: That is the dependency ratio.

questions.stem: The authors' point that 'individual choices operated within, and were constrained by, structural conditions' reflects which sociological tension?
questions.explanation: The interplay between social constraints (structure) and individual choice (agency) is the structure-agency debate. Nature-nurture concerns genes vs. environment, reliability-validity concerns measurement, and primacy-recency concerns memory.

subquestions.stem: 'Structure' refers to which, and 'agency' to which?
subquestions.explanation: Structure = constraints; agency = individual choice.

subquestions.stem: Saying choices are shaped by constraints emphasizes the role of:
subquestions.explanation: Constraint-focused claims emphasize structure.

passages.passage: Discrete questions (no associated passage). Each item below is a standalone question testing a single concept in the psychological foundations of behavior (AAMC Foundational Concepts 6-7), mirroring the discrete questions interspersed between passages on the real P/S exam. Concepts are grounded in OpenStax Psychology 2e.

passage_source.name: OpenStax Psychology 2e (Chs. 5-12 (discrete items))

questions.stem: Which structures convert light into neural signals in the retina?
questions.explanation: Rods and cones are the retinal photoreceptors that transduce light into neural signals. Hair cells transduce sound in the cochlea, olfactory receptors transduce smell, and Pacinian corpuscles transduce pressure/vibration.

subquestions.stem: Transduction is converting a physical stimulus into what?
subquestions.explanation: Transduction yields a neural signal the brain can use.

subquestions.stem: In the eye, the photoreceptors are the:
subquestions.explanation: Rods and cones are the light-sensing photoreceptors.

questions.stem: A child who cannot yet grasp that pouring water into a taller, thinner glass keeps the amount constant lacks:
questions.explanation: Conservation is understanding that quantity stays constant despite changes in appearance; it is typically absent in Piaget's preoperational stage. Object permanence (sensorimotor) is knowing objects exist when unseen, formal operations involve abstract reasoning, and theory of mind is understanding others' mental states.

subquestions.stem: Understanding that quantity stays the same despite a change in shape is:
subquestions.explanation: That is conservation.

subquestions.stem: Conservation is typically acquired in Piaget's ___ stage.
subquestions.explanation: Concrete operational children master conservation.

questions.stem: Judging that a shy, detail-oriented person is more likely a librarian than a salesperson, while ignoring how many more salespeople there are, reflects the:
questions.explanation: The representativeness heuristic judges probability by similarity to a prototype/stereotype while neglecting base rates. The availability heuristic uses ease of recall, anchoring fixates on an initial value, and framing concerns how options are worded.

subquestions.stem: Judging probability by how well something matches a prototype/stereotype is the ___ heuristic.
subquestions.explanation: Similarity-to-prototype judgments use representativeness.

subquestions.stem: Judging probability by how easily examples come to mind is the ___ heuristic.
subquestions.explanation: Ease-of-recall judgments use availability.

questions.stem: Vivid dreaming, rapid eye movements, and an EEG resembling wakefulness most characterize:
questions.explanation: REM sleep features vivid dreaming, rapid eye movements, and a low-voltage, fast (near-waking) EEG with skeletal-muscle atonia. NREM stage 3 shows slow delta waves, and stage 1 / the hypnagogic state is the light transition into sleep.

subquestions.stem: Deep, slow-wave (delta) sleep is which type?
subquestions.explanation: Slow-wave delta sleep is NREM stage 3.

subquestions.stem: The stage with vivid dreams and paradoxical near-waking brain activity is:
subquestions.explanation: REM is 'paradoxical sleep' with active, waking-like EEG.

questions.stem: A slot machine that pays off after an unpredictable number of plays uses which schedule, known for high, steady responding that resists extinction?
questions.explanation: A variable-ratio schedule reinforces after an unpredictable number of responses and produces high, steady, extinction-resistant responding - the gambling pattern. Fixed-ratio reinforces after a set count, and interval schedules reinforce based on time elapsed.

subquestions.stem: Reinforcement after a set NUMBER of responses vs. a varying number is:
subquestions.explanation: Ratio schedules count responses; 'set' = fixed, 'varying' = variable.

subquestions.stem: Which schedule produces the highest, most extinction-resistant responding?
subquestions.explanation: Variable-ratio yields the strongest, most persistent responding.

passages.passage: Discrete questions (no associated passage). Each item below is a standalone question testing a single concept in the social foundations of behavior and society (AAMC Foundational Concepts 7-10), mirroring the discrete questions on the real P/S exam. Concepts are grounded in OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e and OpenStax Psychology 2e.

passage_source.name: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e (Chs. 1-21 (discrete items))

questions.stem: In studies where participants delivered what they believed were increasingly severe shocks because an authority instructed them to, most complied. This demonstrates:
questions.explanation: Following direct orders from an authority figure is obedience, the focus of Milgram's studies. Conformity is matching peers without orders, the bystander effect is reduced helping with more witnesses, and social loafing is reduced effort in groups.

subquestions.stem: Following direct orders from an authority is ___; matching peers' behavior is ___.
subquestions.explanation: Orders -> obedience; peer matching -> conformity.

subquestions.stem: The classic obedience studies were conducted by:
subquestions.explanation: Milgram ran the obedience experiments; Asch studied conformity.

questions.stem: Agreeing to a small request first makes people more likely to agree to a larger request later. This persuasion technique is:
questions.explanation: Foot-in-the-door starts with a small request to increase later compliance with a larger one. Door-in-the-face starts large then retreats to smaller, lowballing changes the deal after agreement, and the reciprocity norm involves returning favors.

subquestions.stem: Starting with a small request to gain later compliance with a bigger one is:
subquestions.explanation: Small-then-large is foot-in-the-door.

subquestions.stem: Starting with a large request, then retreating to a smaller one, is:
subquestions.explanation: Large-then-small is door-in-the-face.

questions.stem: A student who credits an A to their intelligence but blames an F on an unfair professor shows the:
questions.explanation: The self-serving bias attributes one's successes to internal factors and failures to external factors, protecting self-esteem. The fundamental attribution error and actor-observer bias concern explaining others' vs. one's own behavior generally, and the just-world hypothesis is believing people get what they deserve.

subquestions.stem: Taking credit for successes but blaming failures on outside causes protects:
subquestions.explanation: The pattern serves and protects the self.

subquestions.stem: This attribution pattern is the ___ bias.
subquestions.explanation: It is the self-serving bias.

questions.stem: In the Strange Situation, an infant who explores freely, is distressed at separation, and is quickly comforted at reunion shows which attachment style?
questions.explanation: Secure attachment is marked by using the caregiver as a base for exploration, distress at separation, and easy comforting at reunion. Avoidant infants show little distress or contact-seeking, anxious-ambivalent infants are hard to soothe, and disorganized infants show contradictory behavior.

subquestions.stem: The Strange Situation, developed by Mary Ainsworth, measures infant:
subquestions.explanation: It assesses attachment style.

subquestions.stem: An infant easily soothed by the caregiver at reunion is ___ attached.
subquestions.explanation: Easy comforting at reunion indicates secure attachment.

questions.stem: Emile Durkheim's concept for a breakdown of social norms and the resulting sense of normlessness is:
questions.explanation: Durkheim's anomie is normlessness arising when social regulation breaks down. Alienation and false consciousness are Marxian concepts (estrangement from labor and misperception of one's class interests), and the sick role is Parsons's illness concept.

subquestions.stem: Durkheim (a functionalist) coined the term for normlessness:
subquestions.explanation: Normlessness = anomie (Durkheim).

subquestions.stem: Marx's term for workers' estrangement from their labor is:
subquestions.explanation: Estrangement from labor = alienation (Marx).

questions.stem: The demographic transition model describes a society shifting from:
options: low fertility to permanently high fertility
urban living back to rural living
high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates
questions.explanation: The demographic transition moves from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as societies industrialize, with a middle phase of rapid growth when death rates fall before birth rates. The other options reverse or misstate the model.

subquestions.stem: Early in the transition, death rates fall while birth rates stay high, so the population:
subquestions.explanation: The gap between high births and falling deaths causes rapid growth.

subquestions.stem: Late in the transition, both birth and death rates are:
subquestions.explanation: The end state is low births and low deaths.

questions.stem: The belief that social positions are earned purely through talent and effort, independent of inherited advantages, is the ideology of:
questions.explanation: Meritocracy is the belief that rewards track individual talent and effort. Evidence of low mobility and social reproduction challenges a pure meritocracy claim. Anomie is normlessness, and the other options are unrelated population or group-behavior concepts.

subquestions.stem: 'Meritocracy' claims rewards go to people based on:
subquestions.explanation: Meritocracy attributes outcomes to individual merit.

subquestions.stem: Evidence of low mobility and social reproduction does what to a pure meritocracy claim?
subquestions.explanation: Persistent inherited advantage undercuts pure meritocracy.

passages.passage:
Is there any knowledge in the world so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it? This question, which at first sight might not seem difficult, is really among the most difficult that can be asked. In daily life we assume as certain many things which, on closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent contradictions that only a great deal of thought enables us to know what it is that we may really believe.

Consider the plain table before me. To the eye it appears rectangular, brown, and shiny; to the touch it is smooth, cool, and hard; when I tap it, it gives out a wooden sound. Anyone else who sees, feels, and hears the table will agree with this description, so it might seem that no difficulty could arise. But the moment we try to be more precise, our troubles begin. Although I believe that the table is 'really' of one uniform brown, the parts that reflect the light look far brighter than the rest, and some parts look white because of reflected light. If I move, the parts that reflect the light change, so that the apparent distribution of colours upon the table shifts. It follows that if several people look at the table at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of colours, for no two can view it from precisely the same point, and any change in the point of view changes the way in which the light is reflected.

For most practical purposes these differences are unimportant, but to the painter they are all-important: the painter has to unlearn the habit of thinking that things seem to have the colour which common sense says they 'really' have, and to learn the habit of seeing things as they appear. Here we already meet with one of the distinctions that cause the most trouble in philosophy — the distinction between 'appearance' and 'reality,' between what things seem to be and what they are. The table, if it is 'real' at all, must have some real colour; yet the colour we see is not a property of the table in itself but something depending upon the table, the observer, and the way the light falls. When, in ordinary life, we speak of the colour of the table, we mean only the sort of colour which it will seem to have to a normal spectator, under ordinary conditions of light, from an ordinary point of view. But the other colours which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and so, to avoid favouritism, we are compelled to deny that the table has any one particular colour.

The same holds for the texture. With the naked eye the grain of the wood looks smooth and even; under a microscope it shows roughness, and hills and valleys, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to unaided sight. Which of these is the 'real' table? We are naturally tempted to say that what we see through the microscope is more real; yet a still more powerful instrument would reveal something different again, so that we can never rest content with what the eye alone reports. Thus confidence in the senses, which had seemed so secure, begins to desert us.

It becomes evident that the real table, if there is one, is not the same as what we immediately experience by sight or touch or hearing. The real table, if it exists, is not immediately known to us at all, but must be an inference from what is immediately known. Hence two very difficult questions at once arise: Is there a real table at all? And if so, what sort of object can it be?

passage_source.name: Bertrand Russell, 'The Problems of Philosophy' (1912), Ch. 1, adapted

questions.stem: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to:
options: show that even an apparently simple object raises a distinction between appearance and reality
demonstrate that the senses cannot be trusted to reveal any truth about the world
argue that painters perceive objects more accurately than ordinary observers do
establish that the real table is uniformly brown, rectangular, and smooth
questions.explanation: The passage opens with a general question about certainty but immediately grounds it in the concrete table in order to develop 'the distinction between appearance and reality' — that development is its purpose (A). (B) overstates the text: the author says confidence 'begins to desert us' and still holds that a real table may be reached by inference, not that the senses reveal no truth. (C) misuses the painter, who is said to see things 'as they appear,' not more truly than they really are. (D) contradicts the passage, which denies the table has any one real colour or texture.

subquestions.stem: Does the passage stay abstract, or does it work from a specific object?
options: It works from one concrete object (a table) toward a broader philosophical point
It only ever discusses knowledge in the abstract
subquestions.explanation: After the opening question, the whole argument is built on the concrete table example.

subquestions.stem: What key distinction does the table example introduce?
subquestions.explanation: The author explicitly names 'the distinction between appearance and reality.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, we are 'compelled to deny that the table has any one particular colour' because:
options: colour is an illusion that exists only inside the observer's mind
the colours seen under different conditions each have an equal claim to reality, so none can be privileged
only the report of a normal spectator under ordinary conditions should count
observers disagree about the table's shape rather than about its colour
questions.explanation: The author states that the colours appearing under other conditions 'have just as good a right to be considered real,' so that 'to avoid favouritism' no single colour can be assigned (B). (A) is never claimed; the author says colour depends on table, observer, and light, not that it is mere illusion. (C) inverts the point — the normal-spectator report is a convenient convention, not the reason the table lacks one real colour. (D) misattributes the disagreement to shape.

subquestions.stem: Do colours seen under different conditions have different claims to being 'real'?
options: No — each has 'just as good a right to be considered real'
Yes — the brightest appearance is the most real
subquestions.explanation: The passage grants every appearance an equal right to be called real.

subquestions.stem: If no single condition's colour is privileged, what follows about 'the' colour of the table?
options: Its true colour is the average of all its appearances
It cannot be assigned any one particular colour
subquestions.explanation: Refusing to favour any appearance forces the denial of a single real colour.

questions.stem: Within the argument, the reference to the microscope serves chiefly to:
options: prove that scientific instruments finally reveal the real table
show that the table's roughness is more real than its smoothness
extend the appearance/reality problem from colour to texture, undermining reliance on the naked eye
suggest that only trained scientists can perceive reality
questions.explanation: The microscope discussion moves the problem from colour to texture, showing the naked eye is no more authoritative than the instrument (C). (B) is the tempting trap the author explicitly rejects: 'a still more powerful instrument would reveal something different again,' so roughness is not 'more real.' (A) is rejected for the same reason. (D) about scientists is unsupported.

subquestions.stem: Before the microscope, which property was under discussion? After it?
options: Only the sound of the table
subquestions.explanation: The microscope paragraph shifts the same worry onto texture.

subquestions.stem: Does the author treat the microscope's image as the 'real' table?
options: No — a still more powerful instrument would show something different again
Yes — the microscope reveals the table as it really is
subquestions.explanation: Each stronger instrument yields yet another appearance, so none is final.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the reliability of the senses is best described as:
options: contemptuous dismissal of everything they report
initial confidence giving way to reasoned doubt
questions.explanation: Confidence in the senses 'had seemed so secure' but 'begins to desert us' — a movement from confidence to doubt (D). (A) and (B) are opposite extremes the measured prose avoids; the author neither fully trusts nor sneeringly dismisses the senses. (C) ignores the author's evident, careful engagement with the question.

subquestions.stem: At the outset, how secure did confidence in the senses seem?
subquestions.explanation: The passage says that confidence 'had seemed so secure.'

subquestions.stem: By the end of the passage, what happens to that confidence?
subquestions.explanation: The closing movement is toward doubt, not confirmation.

questions.stem: Two observers standing in different places both insist they see 'the same brown table.' The author would most likely respond that they:
options: agree only about the colour a normal spectator would report under ordinary conditions, not about identical immediate experiences
are both simply mistaken about whether the table exists at all
cannot both be right: one perceives the real table and the other an illusion
have proven, by their agreement, that the table has one real colour after all
questions.explanation: The passage says that in ordinary life 'the colour of the table' means only the colour a normal spectator would report under ordinary conditions; since 'no two can view it from precisely the same point,' they cannot share identical immediate experiences (A). (B) overstates — existence is a separate question raised only at the very end. (C) imposes a real/illusion split the author avoids. (D) contradicts the denial that the table has one real colour.

subquestions.stem: When ordinary people speak of 'the colour of the table,' what does the passage say they mean?
options: Their private immediate sensation, which is identical for everyone
The colour a normal spectator would report under ordinary conditions
subquestions.explanation: The author defines the everyday phrase in terms of a normal spectator's report.

subquestions.stem: Can two people in different positions have identical immediate colour-experiences here?
options: No — no two can view it from precisely the same point
Yes — position makes no difference to what is seen
subquestions.explanation: Different viewpoints necessarily change the reflected light and thus the appearance.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most WEAKEN the author's claim that the real table 'must be an inference from what is immediately known'?
options: A more powerful microscope reveals yet another surface texture
Observers can, under controlled conditions, directly perceive the table's intrinsic properties without any inference
People from different cultures use different words for the table's colour
The table looks brighter in the places where the light reflects off it
questions.explanation: The claim is that the real table is reached only by inference from immediate experience; a demonstration that its intrinsic properties can be perceived directly would remove the need for inference and thus weaken it (B). (A) and (D) are simply further appearances that support the author. (C) concerns vocabulary, not whether perception is inferential.

subquestions.stem: State the claim to be weakened.
options: The table is a shade of brown
The real table is known only by inference, never immediately
subquestions.explanation: Identify the target claim before testing what would undercut it.

subquestions.stem: Which kind of finding would undercut 'known only by inference'?
options: Evidence that the table's real properties can be perceived directly
Evidence of yet another appearance under a new instrument
subquestions.explanation: Direct perception would bypass the inference the claim insists upon; another appearance would only reinforce it.

passages.passage:
Among the most contested claims in moral philosophy is the assertion that ethical judgments are irreducibly relative to the cultural frameworks that produce them. Cultural relativism, in its strongest form, holds not merely that different societies happen to endorse different moral codes, but that no standpoint outside all cultures exists from which those codes can be objectively ranked. If morality is constituted by social practice rather than discovered through reason or intuition, then condemning another culture's practices amounts to little more than projecting one's own conventions onto alien terrain.

Defenders of this position often draw strength from the anthropological record, which reveals a startling diversity of moral norms across societies separated by time and geography. Practices that one tradition regards as obligatory — ancestor veneration, dowry exchange, arranged marriage — strike others as superstitious, exploitative, or coercive. From this diversity, relativists infer that no norm enjoys a privileged status independent of its cultural home. To insist otherwise, they argue, is to mistake familiarity for objectivity.

Yet the relativist position encounters formidable internal difficulties. If moral judgments are valid only within the culture that generates them, then the reformer who criticizes her own society's practices — the abolitionist in a slave-holding nation, the suffragette in a society that bars women from public life — is simply wrong by definition. Her protest cannot be morally correct because the dominant convention of her society says otherwise. This consequence strikes many philosophers as a reductio ad absurdum: a moral theory that silences the reformer and vindicates the oppressor cannot be adequate.

Universalists reply that moral diversity, while real, does not demonstrate moral relativism any more than disagreement among scientists demonstrates that there are no scientific facts. People may disagree about the boiling point of water and still be wrong; analogously, cultures may disagree about the permissibility of torture yet one of them may be mistaken. The universalist identifies certain core norms — prohibitions on gratuitous cruelty, requirements of basic reciprocity — that appear in some form across virtually every known society, suggesting not conventional agreement but convergent recognition of genuine moral truths.

The exchange rarely ends there. Relativists counter that the universalist's alleged core norms are either too thin to settle any real dispute or are honored more in word than in deed. Nearly every society condemns killing, they concede — yet societies differ profoundly over which killings count as murder, whom the prohibition protects, and when violence becomes duty. A principle so abstract that rival cultures can all recite it while behaving in opposite ways, the relativist argues, marks no genuine agreement at all. Universalists answer that shared abstract commitments are precisely what one would expect if morality tracked real but imperfectly grasped values, and that quarrels over application no more dissolve an underlying norm than disputed measurements dissolve the quantity being measured.

A nuanced middle position distinguishes between first-order moral claims (what is right or wrong) and metaethical claims (what makes moral judgments true or false). One may acknowledge deep cultural variation in first-order norms while still holding that some metaethical framework — natural law, contractualism, or sentimentalism — provides a transcultural criterion of moral evaluation. On this view, the diversity of moral codes is evidence of human fallibility and limited information, not of the absence of any moral standard. Whether such a criterion is ultimately defensible remains among the central unresolved questions of moral philosophy.

passage_source.name: original

questions.stem: According to the passage, the strongest form of cultural relativism claims that:
options: all moral codes are equally good and should be respected without criticism
cultural diversity proves that moral reformers are always mistaken
no perspective exists from which different moral codes can be objectively compared
anthropological fieldwork has confirmed that moral universalism is false
questions.explanation: (C) is correct: the passage defines strong relativism as the view that 'no standpoint outside all cultures exists from which those codes can be objectively ranked.' (A) conflates relativism with a tolerationist prescription the passage does not assert. (B) is a consequence the passage attributes to relativism as a criticism (the reformer problem), not a definition of relativism. (D) misrepresents the argument: the passage says relativists 'draw strength' from anthropological diversity but does not claim fieldwork conclusively confirms relativism.

subquestions.stem: What does the passage say the strongest relativist claim is about?
options: The equal practical value of every moral code
The absence of any neutral vantage point to rank moral codes
subquestions.explanation: The passage's definition focuses on the impossibility of an objective ranking standpoint.

subquestions.stem: Does the passage present anthropological diversity as proving relativism or merely supporting it?
options: As evidence relativists cite in their favor, not as proof
As conclusive proof that relativism is true
subquestions.explanation: The passage says relativists 'draw strength from' the record, not that it proves their view.

questions.stem: The author introduces the abolitionist and suffragette examples primarily to:
options: show that moral reformers are typically proven correct by history
demonstrate that strong moral convictions can survive cultural disapproval
argue that relativism is incompatible with historical progress
illustrate a consequence of relativism that the author implies undermines the theory
questions.explanation: (D) is correct: the examples are deployed to generate the 'reductio ad absurdum' — if relativism is true, reformers who challenge their own society's norms are by definition wrong, which the author calls a devastating consequence. (A) and (C) introduce historical-progress claims the passage does not make. (B) is plausible but too psychological; the passage uses the examples as a logical critique of relativism, not a comment on reformers' personal resolve.

subquestions.stem: What happens to internal reformers if strong relativism is true?
options: They are justified because they appeal to universal human rights
They are, by definition, morally wrong because their society's dominant norm says so
subquestions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that on relativism the reformer 'cannot be morally correct because the dominant convention of her society says otherwise.'

subquestions.stem: What label does the author give to this consequence of relativism?
subquestions.explanation: The author calls it 'a reductio ad absurdum: a moral theory that silences the reformer.'

questions.stem: The universalist analogy comparing moral disagreement to scientific disagreement is intended to show that:
options: disagreement about a claim does not prove there is no fact of the matter
moral philosophy should adopt the methods of natural science
cultures that disagree about morality are engaged in pseudo-disputes
moral progress follows the same pattern as scientific progress
questions.explanation: (A) is correct: the universalist uses the boiling-point example to argue that 'disagreement among scientists [does not demonstrate] that there are no scientific facts,' and the same applies to moral facts. (B) is not implied — the analogy concerns the logic of disagreement, not methodology. (C) inverts the point. (D) introduces a developmental claim the passage does not assert.

subquestions.stem: In the universalist's analogy, what corresponds to moral disagreement?
options: Scientific disagreement about an empirical fact like the boiling point of water
Political disagreement about which party should govern
subquestions.explanation: The passage draws the explicit parallel: scientists may disagree about the boiling point yet one can be wrong.

subquestions.stem: What conclusion does the universalist draw from this analogy?
options: Cultures that disagree about morality are equally correct
Moral disagreement is compatible with there being genuine moral facts
subquestions.explanation: The logic is: disagreement does not equal no fact; therefore moral disagreement does not prove moral relativism.

questions.stem: The 'nuanced middle position' described in the final paragraph holds that:
options: both relativism and universalism are ultimately incoherent and should be abandoned
variation in first-order norms may coexist with a transcultural metaethical criterion
metaethical frameworks must be derived from anthropological observation
cultural diversity in moral norms provides strong evidence against all metaethical theories
questions.explanation: (B) is correct: the middle position separates first-order questions (what is right) from metaethical questions (what makes judgments true), allowing cultural variation at the first level while preserving a universal standard at the second. (A) is not stated. (C) reverses the relationship. (D) contradicts the passage, which interprets diversity as evidence of fallibility.

subquestions.stem: What two levels of moral inquiry does the middle position distinguish?
options: First-order claims (what is right) and metaethical claims (what makes judgments true)
Descriptive claims (what cultures do) and normative claims (what cultures should do)
subquestions.explanation: The passage explicitly names 'first-order moral claims' and 'metaethical claims' as the two levels.

subquestions.stem: How does this middle position interpret widespread moral disagreement?
options: As proof that moral relativism is correct at both levels
As evidence of human fallibility and limited information, not the absence of moral standards
subquestions.explanation: The passage states: 'diversity of moral codes is evidence of human fallibility and limited information, not of the absence of any moral standard.'

questions.stem: A moral relativist would be MOST likely to find which of the following arguments persuasive?
options: The fact that widespread cross-cultural prohibitions on murder exist suggests those prohibitions track a genuine moral truth
Reformers who oppose slavery in slave-holding societies demonstrate that universal moral standards can be recognized
A society that endorses human sacrifice is simply expressing different values, not making an error
Moral disagreement across cultures arises from factual disagreements rather than genuine differences in values
questions.explanation: (C) is correct: relativists hold that a culture's norms are valid within that culture, so a society endorsing human sacrifice is just expressing different values — not wrong. (A) supports universalism by treating cross-cultural convergence as evidence of moral truth. (B) supports universalism by validating the reformer who appeals to universal standards. (D) is a universalist move: if disagreements are merely factual, underlying moral agreement could be reached.

subquestions.stem: What is the core relativist claim about a culture's norms?
options: They are valid within their cultural context and cannot be objectively ranked against others
They are valid only if they agree with universal human rights standards
subquestions.explanation: Relativism holds norms are valid relative to their cultural home, with no external ranking possible.

subquestions.stem: Why does option (A) support universalism rather than relativism?
options: Because it treats cultural diversity as evidence of moral relativism
Because it treats cross-cultural convergence as evidence of an objective moral truth
subquestions.explanation: Finding cross-cultural prohibitions and inferring they reflect a moral truth is exactly the universalist move.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the relativist's use of anthropological diversity as evidence for relativism?
options: Anthropologists routinely misinterpret foreign practices because of their own cultural biases
The academic discipline of anthropology originated in colonial contexts that shaped its methods
Some moral philosophers argue that anthropological data is irrelevant to metaethics
Despite surface variation, all known societies share a core prohibition on inflicting suffering for no reason
questions.explanation: (D) most directly weakens the relativist inference: if a core norm appears universally, the diversity the relativist relies on is superficial, supporting universalism. (A) would cast doubt on data reliability but not directly undermine relativism. (B) raises sociological concerns, not logical ones. (C) supports ignoring the evidence but does not show it fails to support relativism.

subquestions.stem: What inference do relativists draw from anthropological diversity?
options: That no moral code has a privileged status independent of its cultural home
That all cultures must eventually converge on the same moral norms
subquestions.explanation: Relativists use diversity to argue that no norm enjoys objective standing beyond its culture.

subquestions.stem: How would universal cross-cultural agreement on a core norm undermine this inference?
options: It would show that cultures are more similar than anthropologists claim
It would show that some norms may transcend culture, suggesting objective moral standards
subquestions.explanation: A universal norm is exactly what the universalist predicts — it undermines the claim that all norms are merely culturally local.

passages.passage:
Few debates in literary theory have proved more durable than the question of authorial intent: does the meaning of a text reside primarily in what its author meant to communicate, or does meaning emerge through the activity of reading itself? At one extreme, the intentionalist holds that misreading is always possible — that interpretations diverging from the author's design are simply mistaken, however ingenious or culturally resonant they may be. At the other extreme, the anti-intentionalist insists that once a text is released into the world, the author's psychological states become strictly irrelevant: what the words mean is fixed not by biography but by the conventions of the language and genre in which they are embedded.

The anti-intentionalist position gained influential expression in mid-twentieth-century criticism, when theorists argued that treating the author's intention as the criterion of correct interpretation commits a category error. Evidence about what a poet hoped to achieve, they maintained, cannot settle what a poem achieves, because a poem is a verbal artifact that may realize meanings its creator did not foresee — meanings that become available only through the community of readers over time. The celebrated example of an ironic text serves as illustration: a writer may compose a scathing satire of nationalistic rhetoric while sincerely believing the rhetoric they are parodying; the satiric meaning is there in the text whether the author intended it or not.

Intentionalists counter that language is an intentional practice: utterances mean what speakers mean by them, and written language does not somehow escape this fundamental feature of linguistic communication. To read a text in complete disregard of what its author was trying to do, they argue, is to treat it as a natural object rather than a human creation — to decode it the way one might decode an accidental inkblot rather than a deliberate message. Moreover, intentionalists point out that appeals to 'the language and genre' still presuppose communicative conventions that are themselves constituted by the intentions of the linguistic community.

A mediating view distinguishes between actual authorial intention (the historical individual's specific psychological states) and what might be called the implied author: the authorial persona that a competent reader constructs from the textual evidence alone. On this account, interpretation aims neither at private biography nor at free-floating textual play but at the coherent communicative project that the text itself invites. The implied author is, in effect, the best hypothesis about what an ideally communicative author of this text would have intended — a construct that disciplines interpretation without requiring access to historical documents.

What unites all parties to this dispute is the recognition that texts are not transparent windows onto authors' minds or onto a language-independent reality. They are artifacts whose significance is never simply given but must always be construed — a fact that makes hermeneutics, the theory of interpretation, as much a practical as a philosophical discipline.
