passages.passage:
History is not the past itself but a selective reconstruction of the past, assembled from fragmentary evidence by scholars whose questions, categories, and assumptions are inevitably shaped by their own time and place. This observation, often associated with the philosophy of history that emerged in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, does not reduce historical writing to fiction. Yet it does demand that historians acknowledge their craft as an interpretive one rather than a neutral transcription of what happened.

The most influential historians have always made choices: choices about which events to emphasize, which actors to foreground, and which causal chains to trace. A military historian who concentrates on battles and generals produces a different account of the same period than a social historian who foregrounds the lives of ordinary laborers, or an economic historian who treats fluctuations in grain prices as the deeper explanatory variable. None of these accounts is simply wrong; each illuminates a dimension of a complex past while necessarily leaving other dimensions in shadow.

Critics of this pluralism worry that it licenses an anything-goes relativism in which no historical account is better than any other. Defenders respond that recognizing the constructed character of historical narratives is compatible with rigorous standards of evidence, logical consistency, and fidelity to the archival record. An interpretation can be shown to be false if it contradicts well-authenticated documents, or shown to be weak if it ignores a large body of relevant evidence. The standards are not arbitrary, even if the questions that animate historical inquiry are themselves products of particular intellectual climates.

A further complication arises from the role of the historical archive itself. Archives are not neutral repositories of the past; they are collections shaped by decisions about what to preserve, who had the resources to produce written records, and which categories of information administrative systems deemed worth tracking. Consequently, the voices most abundantly represented in archives tend to be those of literate elites, state bureaucracies, and dominant institutions, while the experiences of the illiterate, the dispossessed, and the colonized are filtered through the records of those who observed or administered them from a position of power.

Contemporary historians have developed a range of techniques to recover marginalized perspectives: reading documents 'against the grain' of their intended purpose, triangulating between different types of sources, and drawing on oral traditions and material culture as complementary evidence. These methods have expanded the scope of historical knowledge considerably, even as they have deepened awareness that the gap between the past and the historian's account of it can never be fully closed.

None of this counsels despair about historical knowledge. The recognition that every history is written from somewhere, on the basis of imperfect and unevenly preserved traces, is better understood as a discipline than as a defeat. It obliges the historian to state her guiding questions openly, to weigh the silences of the record as carefully as its assertions, and to hold her conclusions as revisable in the light of new evidence or sharper questions. Readers, for their part, are invited to judge a historical account not by whether it achieves an impossible neutrality but by the range of evidence it engages, the rival explanations it takes seriously, and the candor with which it marks the limits of what it cannot know.

passages.passage:
Beauty and sublimity are often treated as synonyms in everyday speech, but the aesthetic tradition has long maintained a crucial distinction between them. Beauty, on the classical account, is associated with harmony, proportion, and pleasure: the beautiful object is one whose parts cohere in a way that the observer finds immediately gratifying. Sublimity, by contrast, involves an experience of excess — of forms or magnitudes that exceed the observer's capacity to take them in all at once. The encounter with the sublime is therefore double-edged: it produces both awe and a kind of distress, a sense of being overwhelmed that coexists with exhilaration.

Eighteenth-century theorists were among the first to treat the sublime as a distinct aesthetic category. One influential account located the cause of sublimity in attributes such as vast extent, darkness, and the suggestion of danger or power. A stormy ocean, a jagged mountain range, the interior of a vast cathedral — these provoke a response that differs qualitatively from our response to a well-proportioned garden or a graceful melody. The difference lies not in mere intensity but in the character of the response: the sublime suspends our habitual sense of comfort and security.

A subsequent philosophical tradition shifted the locus of the sublime from the external object to the observer's mental activity. On this view, what is truly sublime is not the mountain itself but the mind's discovery of its own capacity to conceive of what it cannot perceive — to think totality even when the senses are overwhelmed by the magnitude before them. The initial feeling of inadequacy thus gives way to a recognition of the mind's superiority: the faculty that can frame the idea of infinity is, in this sense, greater than any finite spectacle.

These two accounts — one locating sublimity in the object's properties, the other in the observer's cognitive response — are not necessarily incompatible. Objects with certain properties may reliably trigger the cognitive response that constitutes the full experience of the sublime. What both accounts agree on, however, is that the sublime cannot be reduced to beauty: the sublime disrupts the comfortable relationship between the observer and the world, while beauty affirms and soothes it.

The distinction carries an ethical resonance that later writers were quick to draw out. Because the sublime confronts the observer with magnitudes that dwarf the human frame, it has often been tied to humility — to a chastening awareness of finitude that beauty, with its reassurances of order and fit, does not compel. Standing before a storm or an abyss, the spectator is reminded that the world is not arranged for human convenience. And yet, on the observer-centered account, the very same encounter can enlarge the self, for the mind that registers its own smallness is also the mind capacious enough to entertain the immensity that occasions the feeling. This union of abasement and elevation is what makes the sublime so stubbornly resistant to the vocabulary of ordinary pleasure.

Contemporary critics have extended the concept of the sublime to non-natural contexts. The technological sublime finds its occasion in artifacts of overwhelming scale or power: a vast suspension bridge, a particle accelerator, a data center housing more information than any mind could process. Whether such objects genuinely provoke the traditional experience of mingled awe and inadequacy, or whether they produce only spectacle and wonder, remains a live debate in aesthetic theory.

Social capital — broadly understood as the networks of relationships, norms of reciprocity, and trust that enable collective action — has become one of the most debated concepts in contemporary sociology. Proponents argue that it explains why some communities flourish economically and politically while others, equally well endowed in financial and physical resources, remain mired in dysfunction. Where citizens trust one another and are embedded in overlapping civic associations, cooperative ventures are easier to organize, contracts are more reliably honored, and public goods are more effectively maintained.

The concept distinguishes between two broad types. Bonding social capital refers to the dense ties within homogeneous groups — extended families, ethnic neighborhoods, religious congregations — that provide strong mutual support and a sense of belonging. Bridging social capital refers to the weaker but more diverse ties that link members of different social groups, enabling information and resources to flow across community boundaries. Theorists have argued that bridging capital is especially important for economic mobility and democratic stability, because it prevents the insularity and exclusivity that can calcify into tribal antagonism. The interplay between the two forms often matters more than either in isolation. Newcomers to a city, for example, tend to rely first on bonding ties — kin and compatriots who supply lodging, informal credit, and job referrals — and only later cultivate the bridging ties to employers, officials, and institutions beyond their original circle that permit genuine advancement. A community rich in bonding capital but starved of bridging capital may be tightly knit yet economically trapped, whereas one with abundant bridging ties but thin internal solidarity may struggle to sustain the everyday obligations on which cooperation depends. On this view the vitality of a community turns less on how much social capital it can claim than on how its bonding and bridging forms are balanced against each other.

Critics have raised several concerns. First, they argue that the concept is so capacious as to be analytically vacuous: if social capital includes trust, networks, and norms all at once, it risks becoming a label that explains everything and therefore explains nothing. Second, the emphasis on voluntary civic associations may obscure the role of institutional design and state capacity in producing the outcomes attributed to social capital. A society with strong courts, reliable public services, and enforceable property rights may achieve cooperation through formal mechanisms, regardless of the density of its associational life.

A third critique focuses on the dark side of social capital. The same dense ties that produce cohesion within a group can generate exclusion and hostility toward outsiders. Historically, tightly bonded criminal networks, nativist movements, and exclusionary professional guilds have all exhibited strong social capital while causing harm to those outside the charmed circle. If social capital is a neutral resource that amplifies whatever goals a group pursues, then celebrating it uncritically is a mistake. A community of mutual trust can be a community of mutual hostility toward all who fall outside its boundaries, and the literature on ethnic cleansing, organized crime, and racially restrictive covenants demonstrates this possibility in grim historical detail.

These debates have produced a more nuanced research agenda. Scholars now investigate not just the presence or absence of social capital but its distribution across social groups, its articulation with formal institutions, and the conditions under which it promotes rather than undermines democratic participation and social equity.

That social capital reliably promotes beneficial outcomes for society as a whole
That formal institutions are inferior to voluntary associations in generating cooperation
That social capital varies significantly across communities
questions.explanation: (B) is correct: the dark-side critique argues that dense ties can produce exclusion and harm outsiders, undermining the assumption that social capital is universally beneficial. (A) is not directly challenged by this critique. (C) is the second critique, not the dark-side critique. (D) is a sociological observation the passage does not dispute.

subquestions.stem: What examples does the passage give of groups with high social capital that caused harm?
options: Criminal networks, nativist movements, and exclusionary professional guilds
subquestions.explanation: The passage names 'tightly bonded criminal networks, nativist movements, and exclusionary professional guilds.'

subquestions.stem: What does the dark-side critique imply about uncritical celebration of social capital?
options: It is a mistake, because social capital amplifies whatever goals a group pursues
It is justified, because the benefits always outweigh the harms
subquestions.explanation: The passage states: 'If social capital is a neutral resource that amplifies whatever goals a group pursues, then celebrating it uncritically is a mistake.'

questions.stem: A city with low voluntary associational activity but strong courts, reliable police, and efficient public services achieves low corruption and high civic cooperation. This scenario most directly supports which critique of social capital theory?
options: That bridging capital cannot exist without strong bonding capital as a foundation
That social capital is analytically vacuous because it defines terms too broadly
That formal institutional design may produce cooperative outcomes independently of social capital
That the dark side of social capital makes it net-negative for democratic societies
questions.explanation: (C) is correct: the second critique argues that 'a society with strong courts, reliable public services, and enforceable property rights may achieve cooperation through formal mechanisms, regardless of the density of its associational life.' (A) is not a claim in the passage. (B) concerns conceptual breadth, not empirical outcomes. (D) concerns dark-side harms, not institutional mechanisms.

subquestions.stem: What does the second critique argue can substitute for social capital?
options: Increased investment in voluntary civic associations
Strong formal institutions such as courts and reliable public services
subquestions.explanation: The critique says 'a society with strong courts, reliable public services... may achieve cooperation through formal mechanisms.'

subquestions.stem: Does the scenario support or challenge the positive view of social capital?
options: Challenges it, by showing that good outcomes can occur without high social capital
Supports it, by showing that formal institutions build social capital
subquestions.explanation: The city achieves cooperation without dense voluntary associations, suggesting social capital is not necessary.

questions.stem: The passage implies that the more nuanced research agenda described in the final paragraph arose primarily because:
options: scholars discovered that social capital is irrelevant to economic development
government agencies began funding research into civic associations for policy purposes
the distinction between bonding and bridging capital was proven empirically false
the critiques identified in paragraphs three and four revealed significant limitations in earlier approaches
questions.explanation: (D) is implied: 'These debates have produced a more nuanced research agenda' — 'these debates' refers to the critiques. (A) contradicts the passage. (B) is not mentioned. (C) contradicts the passage, which continues to use the bonding/bridging distinction.

subquestions.stem: What does 'these debates' refer to in the final paragraph?
options: The debates between sociologists and economists about whether trust is measurable
The critiques about analytical vacuity, formal institutions, and the dark side of social capital
subquestions.explanation: The passage transitions with 'These debates have produced a more nuanced research agenda,' referring back to paragraphs three and four.

subquestions.stem: What new questions does the nuanced agenda investigate?
options: Distribution of social capital, relation to formal institutions, and conditions under which it promotes democracy
Historical origins of social capital in pre-modern European societies
subquestions.explanation: The passage lists: 'distribution across social groups, articulation with formal institutions, and conditions under which it promotes... democratic participation.'

passages.passage:
Democratic legitimacy, on one influential account, does not derive from the mere aggregation of pre-formed preferences through voting. Rather, it emerges from the quality of the public reasoning that precedes and informs collective decisions. This deliberative ideal holds that citizens who engage in open, reciprocal, and reasoned discourse — genuinely considering one another's arguments rather than simply advocating for prior commitments — are more likely to reach outcomes that are justifiable to all affected parties, regardless of who ultimately wins the vote.

The deliberative model places considerable demands on participants. It requires a willingness to offer reasons that others can evaluate on their merits, not just expressions of passion or assertions of power. It requires a disposition to revise one's views in response to compelling counter-arguments. And it requires conditions of rough equality: if some participants lack the resources, time, or rhetorical confidence to engage effectively, the deliberation is skewed in ways that may reproduce rather than remedy existing inequalities of power.

Critics have challenged the deliberative ideal on several grounds. The most fundamental challenge concerns the status of passionate advocacy. Much of what moves democratic politics — the eloquence of a civil-rights speech, the moral urgency communicated by a protest march, the experiential testimony of those who have suffered injustice — does not take the form of a reasoned argument that invites calm evaluation. To require that all democratic communication conform to deliberative norms risks excluding the voices of the marginalized, whose experiences may be most authentically expressed through modes other than academic debate.

A second critique concerns the domain of the reasonable. Deliberative theory assumes that despite deep disagreements, a set of publicly acceptable reasons can be identified that citizens holding different moral and religious convictions can endorse. Critics argue this assumption is empirically dubious in societies characterized by deep moral pluralism: when citizens disagree not just about policies but about the very framework within which policies should be evaluated, appeals to 'public reason' may function to privilege particular substantive views disguised as neutral procedural ones. The point can be sharpened with an example. When a legislature debates whether assisted dying should be permitted, one citizen may argue from the sanctity of life and another from the primacy of individual autonomy. A demand that each set aside these 'sectarian' premises and reason only from what everyone can accept may sound even-handed, yet in practice it tends to favor whichever background outlook already resembles the supposedly neutral default — often a secular, individualist one. What presents itself as a ground rule for fair discussion, the critics contend, can thus operate as a substantive thesis smuggled in under procedural dress, settling in advance the very questions it claims only to referee.

Defenders of deliberative democracy acknowledge these tensions but argue they point to the need for a more expansive and less rationalist conception of deliberation — one that includes narrative, testimony, and emotional appeal alongside discursive argument — rather than an abandonment of the deliberative ideal itself. If the goal is collective decision-making that citizens can recognize as fair, some approximation of reasoned exchange remains indispensable, even if the form that exchange takes must be more capacious than classical deliberative theory imagined.

questions.stem: According to the deliberative ideal described in the passage, democratic legitimacy comes from:
options: the quality of public reasoning that precedes and informs collective decisions
the numerical majority achieved through fair and transparent vote-counting
the equal distribution of political power among all social groups
the charisma and eloquence of political leaders who can unify citizens
questions.explanation: (A) is stated directly: legitimacy 'emerges from the quality of the public reasoning that precedes and informs collective decisions.' (B) describes aggregative democracy, which the passage contrasts with deliberative democracy. (C) is not the deliberative model's account of legitimacy. (D) is not part of the deliberative ideal.

subquestions.stem: What does the passage contrast with the deliberative model's account of legitimacy?
options: The enforcement of constitutional rights by courts
The mere aggregation of pre-formed preferences through voting
subquestions.explanation: The passage says legitimacy 'does not derive from the mere aggregation of pre-formed preferences through voting.'

subquestions.stem: What quality of public reasoning matters?
options: Open, reciprocal, and genuinely reasoned discourse that considers others' arguments
The persuasiveness of professional rhetoricians hired by political parties
subquestions.explanation: The passage specifies: 'open, reciprocal, and reasoned discourse — genuinely considering one another's arguments.'

questions.stem: Unequal access to deliberative participation is a problem according to the passage because it:
options: violates the procedural requirement that all votes count equally
may reproduce rather than remedy existing power inequalities
ensures that majorities always impose their views on minorities
reduces the number of citizens who engage in civic associations
questions.explanation: (B) is stated: if participation is unequal, 'the deliberation is skewed in ways that may reproduce rather than remedy existing inequalities of power.' (A) conflates deliberation with voting. (C) is not the claim made. (D) relates to social capital themes not discussed here.

subquestions.stem: What conditions does the deliberative model require for legitimate deliberation?
options: Rough equality so that all participants can engage effectively
subquestions.explanation: The passage says deliberation 'requires conditions of rough equality: if some participants lack the resources... the deliberation is skewed.'

subquestions.stem: What happens when some participants lack resources, time, or rhetorical confidence?
options: Deliberation may reproduce rather than remedy existing power inequalities
Citizens tend to vote with economic interests rather than considered judgments
subquestions.explanation: The passage warns the deliberation becomes 'skewed in ways that may reproduce rather than remedy existing inequalities of power.'

questions.stem: Critics who argue that requiring 'public reason' privileges certain substantive views are primarily concerned that:
options: public deliberation inevitably becomes dominated by professional politicians
citizens are unwilling to revise their views after hearing counter-arguments
neutral procedural norms may actually disguise particular moral and religious commitments
majority decisions always fail to respect the rights of religious minorities
questions.explanation: (C) is the critique: 'appeals to public reason may function to privilege particular substantive views disguised as neutral procedural ones.' (A) introduces politicians not mentioned. (B) concerns willingness to revise, discussed as a demand in paragraph two. (D) introduces majority/minority rights, not the public-reason critique.

subquestions.stem: What does the second critique say about the assumption that publicly acceptable reasons exist?
options: Such reasons always exist but are difficult to articulate simply
The assumption is empirically dubious in deeply pluralistic societies
subquestions.explanation: The passage says the assumption is 'empirically dubious in societies characterized by deep moral pluralism.'

subquestions.stem: What does it mean for 'public reason' to privilege a substantive view 'disguised as neutral'?
options: One moral or religious framework gets treated as the universally acceptable standard when it actually reflects a particular worldview
Politicians use technical language to confuse citizens about policy details
subquestions.explanation: The critique is that 'public reason' claims neutrality but actually encodes one framework's assumptions as the default.

questions.stem: A grassroots campaign uses personal storytelling by formerly incarcerated people to shift public opinion on criminal justice reform, deliberately avoiding statistical arguments. A defender of the deliberative ideal would most likely say this campaign:
options: undermines democratic legitimacy because it relies on emotion rather than reasoned argument
is the most powerful form of deliberation because stories are more persuasive than statistics
is only legitimate if the storytellers also provide policy proposals based on empirical evidence
is consistent with an expanded deliberative model that includes narrative and testimony alongside discursive argument
questions.explanation: (D) is correct: defenders call for 'a more expansive and less rationalist conception of deliberation — one that includes narrative, testimony, and emotional appeal alongside discursive argument.' Personal storytelling exemplifies this. (A) represents the narrow rationalist view critics are challenging. (B) is not the passage's claim. (C) introduces a requirement the passage's defenders do not make.

subquestions.stem: What do defenders of deliberative democracy argue in the final paragraph?
options: Deliberation should be restricted to formal academic debate to ensure rigor
Deliberation should be expanded to include narrative, testimony, and emotional appeal, not just discursive argument
subquestions.explanation: Defenders call for 'a more expansive and less rationalist conception of deliberation — one that includes narrative, testimony, and emotional appeal.'

subquestions.stem: Does the final paragraph say the deliberative ideal should be abandoned?
options: No — it calls for a revised, more expansive conception, not abandonment
Yes — the critiques are said to be decisive against deliberative theory
subquestions.explanation: The defenders argue for revision 'rather than an abandonment of the deliberative ideal itself.'

questions.stem: The passage's description of deliberative democracy's demands implies that a deliberative process would be corrupted when participants:
options: assert power or passion instead of offering reasons others can evaluate on their merits
vote according to their sincere preferences after listening to all arguments
invoke constitutional principles as reasons for their positions
change their minds after hearing arguments from the opposing side
questions.explanation: (A) is the inverse of the demand stated: deliberation requires offering 'reasons that others can evaluate on their merits, not just expressions of passion or assertions of power.' When participants substitute passion for reasons, deliberation is corrupted. (B) is expected endpoint behavior. (C) is a form of reason, not corruption. (D) is the desired behavior per the passage.

subquestions.stem: What kind of communication does the deliberative model require?
options: Passionate rhetoric that moves fellow citizens to action
Reasons that others can evaluate on their merits
subquestions.explanation: The model requires 'a willingness to offer reasons that others can evaluate on their merits, not just expressions of passion or assertions of power.'

subquestions.stem: What disposition must deliberators have toward opposing arguments?
options: A willingness to revise their views in response to compelling counter-arguments
A commitment to maintaining their initial positions regardless of counterevidence
subquestions.explanation: The passage says deliberation 'requires a disposition to revise one's views in response to compelling counter-arguments.'

passages.passage:
Ritual occupies a paradoxical place in modern social thought. On one hand, it has been systematically studied as a fundamental mechanism of social solidarity: shared symbolic performances bind participants together, express and reinforce collective values, and mark the transitions — birth, initiation, marriage, death — that punctuate the human life course. On the other hand, modern societies tend to regard ritual with a degree of unease, as if elaborate ceremony were a relic of pre-rational ages unsuited to a world governed by science and voluntary choice.

Early sociological and anthropological accounts emphasized the integrative functions of ritual. Ceremonies, on this view, do not merely reflect an already-existing social order; they actively produce and sustain it. When a community gathers to mark a harvest, a coronation, or a national founding, participants do not simply observe an event — they enact membership in a collectivity that transcends any individual. The shared emotional experience generated by such occasions — what early theorists called collective effervescence — temporarily dissolves the boundaries between self and group, creating a felt sense of unity that persists in social memory long after the ceremony has concluded.

Later anthropologists complicated this functionalist picture by attending to the internal diversity and contestation that characterize real rituals. Ceremonies are rarely performed identically across time or across the different status groups within a community. The ruling class and the subjugated, men and women, elders and youth — each may experience the same ceremony quite differently, and the ritual may serve to reinforce not solidarity across the board but specific hierarchies of power. From this perspective, treating ritual purely as a mechanism of integration ignores its role in legitimating and reproducing asymmetric social arrangements.

A third approach draws attention to ritual's cognitive and communicative dimensions. Rituals encode information in a form — embodied action, sensory symbol, repeated performance — that is particularly durable and memorable. Unlike propositional statements that can be contested or forgotten, knowledge embedded in ritual is resistant to revision precisely because it is experienced rather than merely asserted. This explains why ritual tends to be invoked when other communicative resources fail: in the face of death, catastrophic loss, or radical uncertainty, shared performance provides a structure of meaning that discursive language alone cannot furnish. Grief rituals in particular demonstrate how embodied collective action can sustain communities through episodes of radical disruption that would otherwise threaten social fabric. The contrast with ordinary instruction is telling. A fact conveyed in a lecture can be doubted the moment the lecture ends; a truth rehearsed year after year in fasting, procession, or song is renewed in the body and rarely submitted to cross-examination at all. This is why communities so often entrust their most load-bearing commitments — who belongs, what is owed to the dead, which obligations the future imposes — not to argument but to observance. The very features that make ritual knowledge conservative, and sometimes an obstacle to reform, are also what allow it to hold a group together when argument alone would divide it, carrying shared meaning across generations that never meet.

Each of these accounts captures something genuine. Ritual is simultaneously a mechanism of solidarity, an arena of power and contestation, and a form of embodied knowledge. Understanding any particular ceremony requires attending to all three dimensions and to the historical context that shapes their relative salience.

questions.stem: The concept of 'collective effervescence' is introduced in the passage to explain:
options: the spontaneous dance and music that accompanies harvest festivals
the felt sense of unity generated by shared emotional experience during ceremony
the cognitive knowledge encoded in repeated symbolic performances
the contestation that occurs when different status groups experience the same ritual differently
questions.explanation: (B) is correct: collective effervescence 'temporarily dissolves the boundaries between self and group, creating a felt sense of unity.' (A) is a concrete detail not mentioned. (C) describes the cognitive dimension in paragraph four. (D) describes the later critique of functionalism in paragraph three.

subquestions.stem: Which paragraph introduces the concept of collective effervescence?
options: The fourth paragraph, in the context of ritual's cognitive dimensions
The second paragraph, in the context of integrative/functionalist accounts
subquestions.explanation: The term appears in paragraph two, where early theorists' integrative account is discussed.

subquestions.stem: What effect does collective effervescence produce?
options: A felt sense of unity that persists in social memory after the ceremony
A rational understanding of the community's shared political values
subquestions.explanation: The passage says it 'creates a felt sense of unity that persists in social memory long after the ceremony has concluded.'

questions.stem: The 'later anthropologists' described in paragraph three challenge the functionalist account primarily by arguing that:
options: collective effervescence is a myth that cannot be observed in ethnographic fieldwork
modern societies have successfully replaced ritual with rational legal institutions
ritual can reinforce hierarchies of power rather than solidarity across all participants
all rituals serve purely cognitive rather than social functions
questions.explanation: (C) is the critique: the ritual 'may serve to reinforce not solidarity across the board but specific hierarchies of power.' (A) attacks a concept the passage presents without disputing; the later challenge concerns power, not existence of effervescence. (B) is not their argument. (D) describes the third approach in paragraph four, not the second challenge.

subquestions.stem: What do later anthropologists attend to that functionalists neglected?
options: The statistical frequency with which rituals are performed
Internal diversity and contestation within real rituals
subquestions.explanation: The passage says later anthropologists complicated functionalism 'by attending to the internal diversity and contestation that characterize real rituals.'

subquestions.stem: Who may benefit differentially from the same ceremony?
options: The ruling class versus the subjugated, men versus women, elders versus youth
Scientists versus religious believers in secular societies
subquestions.explanation: The passage names: 'The ruling class and the subjugated, men and women, elders and youth.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, why is knowledge embedded in ritual more durable than propositional knowledge?
options: Because ritual knowledge is written down in sacred texts that survive for centuries
Because ritual is supervised by religious authorities who enforce correct transmission
Because the emotional arousal of ritual permanently alters memory circuits
Because it is experienced in embodied, sensory, and repeated forms rather than merely asserted
questions.explanation: (D) is the passage's argument: ritual encodes knowledge 'in a form — embodied action, sensory symbol, repeated performance — that is particularly durable... resistant to revision precisely because it is experienced rather than merely asserted.' (A) introduces textual preservation not mentioned. (B) introduces religious authority not mentioned. (C) introduces neuroscience not mentioned.

subquestions.stem: What forms does ritual use to encode knowledge?
options: Written scripture, oral recitation, and legal codification
Embodied action, sensory symbol, and repeated performance
subquestions.explanation: The passage lists: 'embodied action, sensory symbol, repeated performance.'

subquestions.stem: Why is experiential knowledge resistant to revision?
options: Because it is lived through the body and senses, making it harder to question than a statement that can simply be contested
Because religious communities excommunicate members who revise ritual knowledge
subquestions.explanation: The passage says ritual knowledge 'is resistant to revision precisely because it is experienced rather than merely asserted.'

questions.stem: A state funeral draws together citizens from rival political factions, who report afterwards feeling temporarily united despite their differences. This phenomenon would best be explained by which account described in the passage?
options: The integrative account, because the shared ceremony produced collective effervescence
The power-hierarchy account, because the funeral reinforces the legitimacy of the political elite
The cognitive account, because the funeral encodes propositional knowledge about succession
None of the accounts, because state funerals are modern inventions outside the passage's scope
questions.explanation: (A) is correct: rival factions feeling 'temporarily united' despite their differences is precisely what the integrative account explains through collective effervescence, which 'temporarily dissolves the boundaries between self and group.' (B) is unsupported by the scenario: the described phenomenon is unity across factions, not the reinforcement of any elite's legitimacy that the power-hierarchy account would require. (C) does not fit, since the scenario turns on felt unity rather than the transmission of propositional knowledge. (D) is false; the passage treats ceremonies like 'a coronation' as within its scope.

subquestions.stem: What does the integrative account predict about shared ritual participation?
options: It reinforces the distinctions between different status groups
It temporarily dissolves boundaries between self and group, creating felt unity
subquestions.explanation: The integrative account holds that collective effervescence 'temporarily dissolves the boundaries between self and group, creating a felt sense of unity.'

subquestions.stem: How does unity 'despite differences' map onto collective effervescence?
options: The shared funeral experience temporarily overcomes political divisions — the hallmark of effervescence
The rivals remain divided even after the funeral, confirming the power-hierarchy account
subquestions.explanation: Unity 'despite differences' is exactly what effervescence produces — temporary dissolution of ordinary social boundaries.

questions.stem: The passage's final paragraph implies that the three accounts of ritual are:
options: in irreconcilable conflict, making a unified theory of ritual impossible
not mutually exclusive — understanding any ritual requires attending to all three dimensions
hierarchically ordered, with the cognitive account superseding the integrative and power accounts
each fully adequate on its own but applicable only to specific cultural contexts
questions.explanation: (B) is the passage's explicit conclusion: 'Each of these accounts captures something genuine. Ritual is simultaneously a mechanism of solidarity, an arena of power and contestation, and a form of embodied knowledge. Understanding any particular ceremony requires attending to all three dimensions.' (A) contradicts this. (C) is not stated. (D) is not stated — the passage implies all three are needed for any ceremony.

subquestions.stem: Does the final paragraph say any single account is fully adequate on its own?
options: Yes — the cognitive account is presented as most complete
No — it says understanding requires all three dimensions
subquestions.explanation: The passage says 'understanding any particular ceremony requires attending to all three dimensions.'

subquestions.stem: What additional factor does the passage add alongside the three dimensions?
options: Historical context that shapes which dimensions are most salient
The socioeconomic status of the community performing the ritual
subquestions.explanation: The passage adds: 'and to the historical context that shapes their relative salience.'

passages.passage:
Classical economic theory rests on a conception of the agent as fundamentally rational: possessed of stable, consistent preferences, capable of processing available information, and motivated to maximize personal utility. This model has extraordinary analytical power. It generates precise, testable predictions and underlies the welfare theorems that have guided economic policy for generations. Yet beginning in the latter decades of the twentieth century, a body of research in behavioral economics accumulated evidence that humans deviate from this ideal in systematic, predictable, and consequential ways.

Among the most robust findings is loss aversion: people respond more strongly to losses than to equivalent gains. The discomfort of losing one hundred dollars is experienced as more intense than the pleasure of gaining the same amount. This asymmetry has significant implications. It helps explain why people hold losing financial assets far longer than rational profit-maximization would recommend — they prefer the pain of waiting to the certain loss of selling. It also explains why contract and policy framings that emphasize avoiding losses are more motivationally effective than those that emphasize equivalent gains.

A second set of findings concerns heuristic judgment under uncertainty. When people lack the time or information to calculate expected values precisely, they rely on cognitive shortcuts that usually suffice but sometimes produce systematic errors. The availability heuristic leads people to estimate the probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind: dramatic events, such as airplane crashes, are overestimated in frequency because they are memorable, while mundane but statistically commoner risks, such as car accidents, are underestimated. The representativeness heuristic leads people to assess probability by how closely an instance resembles a prototypical category member, often ignoring base-rate information entirely. A familiar illustration involves base rates. Told that a quiet, orderly person who loves books was drawn from a group made up mostly of salespeople and only a few librarians, many respondents confidently judge the person a librarian, swayed by resemblance to a stereotype while all but ignoring how rare librarians are in the sample. The mistake is not stupidity but the misfiring of an ordinarily useful strategy: resemblance is frequently a serviceable guide to category membership, and only in cases engineered to pit it against base-rate information does it lead reliably astray. The shortcuts that behavioral research exposes are, in most everyday settings, both fast and surprisingly accurate; they betray us mainly in the artificial problems constructed to reveal their inner workings.

These findings have generated debate about the appropriate policy response. Some argue that behavioral insights justify 'nudging': designing choice environments so that the default option is the one that most people would choose on reflection. Automatic enrollment in retirement savings plans, for instance, exploits the tendency to accept defaults, boosting participation without eliminating freedom of choice. Critics of nudging worry that it is paternalistic, that it manipulates rather than informs, and that it presupposes policymakers know better than individuals what those individuals' reflective preferences actually are.

The behavioral economics literature does not establish that markets always fail or that regulation is always beneficial. It establishes only that the idealized rational actor is an incomplete description of real human psychology, and that understanding how people actually decide is essential to designing institutions that work well in the world as it is.

questions.stem: According to the passage, loss aversion refers to the finding that people:
options: systematically overestimate the probability of losing money in investments
prefer to avoid making any decisions when the outcome is uncertain
feel losses more intensely than equivalent gains
lose interest in a goal once they have made significant progress toward it
questions.explanation: (C) is the direct definition: 'people respond more strongly to losses than to equivalent gains. The discomfort of losing one hundred dollars is experienced as more intense than the pleasure of gaining the same amount.' (A) confuses loss aversion with availability heuristic. (B) describes decision avoidance, not loss aversion. (D) is a goal-related phenomenon not in the passage.

subquestions.stem: What specific comparison illustrates loss aversion?
options: People lose more money in stock markets than they gain over a lifetime
Losing one hundred dollars feels worse than gaining one hundred dollars feels good
subquestions.explanation: The passage uses: 'The discomfort of losing one hundred dollars is experienced as more intense than the pleasure of gaining the same amount.'

subquestions.stem: What investment behavior does loss aversion help explain?
options: Holding losing assets longer than rational profit-maximization recommends
Buying more stocks when the market is rising than when it is falling
subquestions.explanation: The passage says loss aversion 'explains why people hold losing financial assets far longer than rational profit-maximization would recommend.'

questions.stem: The availability heuristic, as described in the passage, causes people to:
options: assess probability by how closely an instance resembles a typical category member
accept whatever option is presented as the default rather than deliberating actively
overweight recent information while discounting older historical data
overestimate the frequency of dramatic, memorable events and underestimate mundane but commoner risks
questions.explanation: (D) is stated directly: airplane crashes are overestimated 'because they are memorable,' while car accidents 'are underestimated.' (A) describes the representativeness heuristic. (B) describes the default-acceptance tendency. (C) is a recency bias not discussed.

subquestions.stem: What does the availability heuristic use as a proxy for probability?
options: How closely an event resembles a prototype
How easily examples of an event come to mind
subquestions.explanation: The passage says people 'estimate the probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind.'

subquestions.stem: Which type of risk does the availability heuristic cause people to underestimate?
options: Mundane but statistically commoner risks, like car accidents
Rare but dramatic events, like airplane crashes
subquestions.explanation: The passage says 'mundane but statistically commoner risks, such as car accidents, are underestimated.'

questions.stem: Critics of nudging worry primarily that it:
options: manipulates rather than informs and presupposes policymakers know better than individuals what those individuals' reflective preferences are
is ineffective because people always override default options when they are aware of them
violates constitutional rights to freedom of economic choice
undermines behavioral economics findings by assuming people are fully rational
questions.explanation: (A) is stated: critics 'worry that it is paternalistic, that it manipulates rather than informs, and that it presupposes policymakers know better than individuals what those individuals' reflective preferences actually are.' (B) is not their critique. (C) introduces constitutional language not in the passage. (D) is the opposite.

subquestions.stem: What term does the passage use to describe critics' concern about policymakers directing behavior?
subquestions.explanation: The passage says critics 'worry that it is paternalistic.'

subquestions.stem: What assumption about policymakers do critics find objectionable?
options: That policymakers know better than individuals what those individuals' reflective preferences actually are
That policymakers are immune to the same cognitive biases as citizens
subquestions.explanation: Critics object to the assumption that nudging 'presupposes policymakers know better than individuals what those individuals' reflective preferences actually are.'

questions.stem: The final paragraph is primarily intended to:
options: argue that behavioral economics has decisively refuted classical economic theory
clarify the limited conclusion behavioral economics supports, distinguishing it from broader claims about market failure
summarize the policy recommendations most behavioral economists endorse
suggest that behavioral findings have not yet accumulated enough evidence to be reliable
questions.explanation: (B) is correct: the passage explicitly states behavioral economics 'does not establish that markets always fail or that regulation is always beneficial. It establishes only that the idealized rational actor is an incomplete description.' (A) contradicts this. (C) is not addressed. (D) contradicts the opening characterization of findings as 'robust.'

subquestions.stem: What does the passage say behavioral economics does NOT establish?
options: That people sometimes deviate from rational decision-making
That markets always fail or that regulation is always beneficial
subquestions.explanation: The passage states: 'The behavioral economics literature does not establish that markets always fail or that regulation is always beneficial.'

subquestions.stem: What limited conclusion does behavioral economics actually support?
options: That the idealized rational actor is an incomplete description of real human psychology
That all economic models should be replaced with psychological ones
subquestions.explanation: It 'establishes only that the idealized rational actor is an incomplete description of real human psychology.'

questions.stem: A health campaign tells people that 'nine out of ten people in your neighborhood have received their flu vaccine' rather than describing the vaccine's medical benefits. This strategy most directly exploits which behavioral finding?
options: Loss aversion, by implying that unvaccinated people are losing something the majority has gained
The availability heuristic, by making vaccine uptake easy to imagine through social examples
The tendency to accept defaults, since vaccination appears to be the expected norm
The representativeness heuristic, by making the unvaccinated person feel unlike a typical neighbor
questions.explanation: (C) is best: the passage describes nudging as designing choice environments around 'the default option [that] is the one that most people would choose,' and telling people that nine of ten neighbors are vaccinated presents vaccination as exactly that expected, majority choice. (A) fails because nothing in the message is framed as a loss relative to a reference point. (B) misapplies the availability heuristic, which concerns judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind, not conforming to what most people do. (D) misapplies the representativeness heuristic, which concerns judging probability by resemblance to a prototype, not social conformity.

subquestions.stem: What does the '9 out of 10 neighbors' framing do to the target audience's perception?
options: It makes the medical risks of flu more vivid and memorable
It makes vaccination appear to be the default norm in their social environment
subquestions.explanation: Telling people the majority is vaccinated presents vaccination as the expected, default behavior — a social norm.

subquestions.stem: Which behavioral finding involves acceptance of default options?
options: The tendency to accept defaults, described in the context of automatic retirement enrollment
Loss aversion, described in the context of holding losing financial assets
subquestions.explanation: The passage describes nudging as 'exploiting the tendency to accept defaults, boosting participation' — as illustrated by automatic retirement enrollment.

passages.passage:
The relationship between mind and body has occupied Western philosophy since antiquity, but the specific problem of consciousness has acquired a new urgency in an era when neuroscience can map the brain in unprecedented detail. Even if we knew the complete physical state of every neuron in a human brain at a given moment, would that knowledge exhaust our understanding of what it is like for the person whose brain it is to be having the experiences they are having? Many philosophers believe the answer is no — and they argue that this gap between complete physical description and subjective experience reveals something fundamental about the nature of mind.

This 'hard problem' — why any physical process should be accompanied by subjective experience at all — is distinguished from the 'easy problems' of consciousness, such as how the brain integrates information, controls attention, or generates verbal reports about mental states. The easy problems are not trivial; they may require decades of research to solve. But they are, in principle, amenable to explanation in functional and computational terms. The hard problem seems to resist this treatment: even a complete functional account of how a system processes information leaves unexplained why processing should feel like anything at all. To feel the force of the puzzle, imagine two systems that process a stimulus in functionally identical ways — the same inputs, the same discriminations, the same outputs — and ask whether it follows that there is something it is like to be each of them, and, if so, whether it must be the same something. Nothing in the functional story, defenders of the hard problem insist, settles the matter: one could in principle specify every computational step by which an auditory system registers a rising tone without thereby explaining why those steps are accompanied by any felt quality at all. It is this apparent slack between function and feeling — not mere complexity — that makes the problem look hard rather than merely unsolved.

Physicalists respond in several ways. Some deny that there is a genuine explanatory gap: what seems like an inexplicable residue is, they argue, an artifact of our limited cognitive access to neural processes rather than evidence of a non-physical dimension of reality. Once neuroscience matures sufficiently, the sense that something has been left out will dissolve, just as vitalism — the doctrine that life requires a special non-physical force — dissolved when biochemistry revealed the mechanisms of metabolism. Others accept that qualia — the intrinsic qualitative character of experience — are real but argue that they are identical with, or constituted by, physical brain states in ways we do not yet fully understand.

Dualists, by contrast, maintain that the hard problem reflects a genuine ontological gap: minds and physical processes belong to categorically different orders of being. This position preserves the intuition that experience is irreducibly subjective but faces the difficulty of explaining how non-physical minds causally interact with physical brains — a puzzle that has shadowed substance dualism since its classical formulation. To say that minds and brains interact is plausible as ordinary description; to explain the mechanism of that interaction without smuggling physical causation back in is a philosophical challenge that has resisted resolution for centuries.

The hard problem of consciousness thus sits at the intersection of metaphysics, philosophy of mind, and neuroscience. Whether it admits of a naturalistic solution remains one of the deepest unresolved questions in intellectual life.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the 'hard problem' of consciousness differs from 'easy problems' in that:
options: easy problems involve subjective experience, while the hard problem involves only brain function
the hard problem has been solved by neuroscience, while easy problems remain outstanding
easy problems are philosophical, while the hard problem is purely empirical
easy problems are amenable to functional explanations, while the hard problem seems to resist explanation in those terms
questions.explanation: (D) is stated: easy problems 'are, in principle, amenable to explanation in functional and computational terms,' while the hard problem 'seems to resist this treatment.' (A) reverses the definitions. (B) is the opposite. (C) reverses their characters.

questions.stem: Some physicalists use the analogy of vitalism to argue that:
options: the apparent inexplicability of consciousness may dissolve as neuroscience matures, just as vitalism dissolved with advances in biochemistry
consciousness is a life-force similar to what vitalists once attributed to living matter
dualists are correct that consciousness cannot be explained by physical processes
neuroscience has already solved the hard problem, as biochemistry solved vitalism
questions.explanation: (A) is the explicit analogy: 'the sense that something has been left out will dissolve, just as vitalism... dissolved when biochemistry revealed the mechanisms of metabolism.' (B) equates consciousness with the discredited vitalist force — the opposite of the physicalists' intent. (C) is the dualist position. (D) is not stated — physicalists are making a future prediction.

subquestions.stem: What happened to vitalism when biochemistry matured?
options: It was refined rather than rejected and is still used in some biological theories
It dissolved — the need for a special non-physical life-force disappeared
subquestions.explanation: The passage says 'vitalism... dissolved when biochemistry revealed the mechanisms of metabolism.'

options: The sense that something has been left out will dissolve
It will become clearer that consciousness is genuinely non-physical
subquestions.explanation: Physicalists argue 'the sense that something has been left out will dissolve, just as vitalism dissolved.'

questions.stem: The passage identifies a specific difficulty that faces substance dualism. This difficulty is:
options: accounting for why different people have similar conscious experiences
explaining how non-physical minds causally interact with physical brains
showing why subjective experience exists at all if minds are non-physical
reconciling dualism with the findings of evolutionary biology
questions.explanation: (B) is stated: dualism 'faces the difficulty of explaining how non-physical minds causally interact with physical brains.' (A) is not mentioned as a specific difficulty. (C) is the hard problem itself, not a unique dualist difficulty. (D) is not mentioned.

They belong to categorically different orders of being

Defining what 'substance' means in modern physics
subquestions.explanation: The passage says: 'explaining how non-physical minds causally interact with physical brains — a puzzle that has shadowed substance dualism since its classical formulation.'

questions.stem: Suppose a neuroscientist fully maps every neural connection and firing pattern during a subject's experience of seeing red. A philosopher who believes the hard problem is genuine would most likely say this mapping:
options: fully explains consciousness, proving that physicalism is correct
provides evidence that qualia do not actually exist
still leaves unexplained what it is like for the subject to experience redness as a subjective quality
shows that the easy problems of consciousness are inseparable from the hard problem
questions.explanation: (C) is correct: the hard-problem philosopher answers no to whether complete physical description exhausts understanding of subjective experience. Even a complete neural map 'leaves unexplained why processing should feel like anything at all.' (A) is the physicalist's hoped-for conclusion. (B) is the eliminativist position. (D) is not a claim in the passage.

subquestions.stem: What question does the hard problem ask?

Why any physical process should be accompanied by subjective experience at all
subquestions.explanation: The hard problem is: 'why any physical process should be accompanied by subjective experience at all.'

subquestions.stem: Does a complete functional or physical account answer this question?
options: No — even a complete functional account leaves unexplained why processing feels like anything
Yes — mapping neural processes fully explains subjective experience
subquestions.explanation: The passage says: 'even a complete functional account of how a system processes information leaves unexplained why processing should feel like anything at all.'

questions.stem: The author's tone toward the hard problem of consciousness is best characterized as:
options: dismissive, suggesting the hard problem will soon be solved by neuroscience
confident that dualism is the correct solution
polemical, arguing that physicalism is obviously mistaken
intellectually serious and genuinely uncertain about its resolution
questions.explanation: (D) is supported throughout: the passage presents multiple positions without endorsing one, describes the problem as 'one of the deepest unresolved questions,' and says 'whether it admits of a naturalistic solution remains' open. (A) is the strong physicalist prediction — presented as one view, not the author's. (B) is false — the passage notes dualism's difficulties. (C) is false — the passage treats physicalism seriously.

No — it presents each with merits and difficulties without endorsing one
subquestions.explanation: The passage presents each view with both its appeal and its challenges, ending with 'remains one of the deepest unresolved questions.'

'The hard problem has been solved by recent advances in computational neuroscience'

passages.passage:
Among the foundational distinctions in the sociology of religion is the division of the world into two mutually exclusive domains: the sacred and the profane. The sacred encompasses all things set apart and forbidden, surrounded by special prohibitions and observed with reverence; the profane designates everything else the ordinary, the utilitarian, the everyday. This distinction is not primarily about supernatural belief. A society without gods can still organize its collective life around sacred objects and practices; conversely, explicitly theistic language can be deployed in contexts so routine that nothing sacred attaches to it at all. The sacred is a structural feature of collective life, not a property of any particular theological tradition.

What makes something sacred is not its intrinsic properties but its relationship to the collective. The sacred object or practice has been designated by the community as set apart, invested with a significance that transcends individual preference and commands a distinctive emotional response. Violations of the sacred provoke not merely practical objection but moral indignation and often the collective sanction of the group. The sacred functions, in this analysis, as a boundary marker: it demarcates what the collective treats as inviolable from what can be freely negotiated, exchanged, or modified. The power of the sacred is thus inseparable from the collective from which it derives and to which it refers. A corollary is that the sacred is hedged about with rules of separation. Precisely because sacred things are set apart, they must be kept from casual contact with the profane: they are approached through prescribed gestures, handled by designated persons, and encountered on appointed occasions rather than at will. Transgression is felt less as a mistake than as a kind of pollution, calling forth rites of purification or punishment rather than simple correction. This logic of separation explains why the sacred can inspire dread as readily as devotion: what is marked off as supremely valuable is also, for that very reason, treated as perilous to handle carelessly. The boundary, in short, is enforced as much by feeling as by rule.

This framework has been applied far beyond explicitly religious contexts. National flags, war memorials, and constitutional documents can function as sacred objects in secular societies: they command a special reverence, their desecration provokes communal outrage, and they focus the collective sense of identity and shared purpose. Academic ceremonies, such as the conferral of degrees and the inauguration of presidents, likewise exhibit a ritualized formality that marks them off from ordinary transactions. The secular and the sacred are not opposites; rather, the sacred is a structural feature of collective life that may attach to entirely secular objects and occasions.

Critics of this framework have worried that extending the concept of the sacred to secular contexts dilutes it beyond usefulness. If anything sufficiently cherished by a community counts as sacred, the concept loses its explanatory precision. Moreover, the framework has been criticized for underplaying internal dissent: in any actual society, which objects are sacred and which are merely important is itself politically contested, and the boundary between the sacred and the profane is drawn by those with the social power to draw it. Sacred designations can thus serve ideological functions, naturalizing existing arrangements by placing them beyond ordinary critical scrutiny.

These tensions notwithstanding, the sacred/profane distinction continues to illuminate the emotional architecture of collective life in ways that strictly rational accounts of social organization cannot easily replicate. Communities that lack shared sacred commitments often struggle to motivate the sacrifices that sustaining collective institutions requires.

The sacred response is purely emotional with no social consequences

passages.passage:
One of the most consequential shifts in twentieth-century philosophy of language was the move away from the view that words get their meaning by standing for objects in the world. On the referentialist picture, to know the meaning of a term like 'gold' is to know which substance the term picks out; to know the meaning of 'Julius Caesar' is to know which historical individual the name refers to. The attractions of this view are obvious: it grounds meaning in something outside language itself, connecting our words to the world they describe and offering a clear criterion for distinguishing correct from incorrect usage.

Yet referentialism encounters serious difficulties when applied to expressions whose meaning does not seem to consist in any reference at all. Words like 'and,' 'perhaps,' 'nevertheless,' and 'of' do not pick out objects, properties, or relations in any obvious sense. Equally problematic are terms whose reference appears to shift depending on context: 'here' refers to wherever the speaker happens to be, 'now' to whenever the utterance is made, and 'I' to whoever is speaking. The meaning of these expressions cannot be their reference, since their reference changes while their meaning remains constant across every ordinary use of the word.

An alternative tradition proposed that meaning is constituted by use. On this view, to know the meaning of a word is not to know what it refers to but to know how to use it -- in what contexts it is appropriately deployed, what inferences it licenses, how it interacts with the meanings of other expressions. This account handles the problematic cases naturally: logical connectives like 'and' are explained by the inferential rules governing their use (the conjunction of P and Q implies both P and Q separately); indexical expressions like 'here' are explained by specifying the rule that they refer to the context of utterance. Knowing the meaning of 'here' means knowing that it picks out the speaker's location, not knowing any particular location.

Critics of the use theory worry that it leaves too little stable content in meaning. If meaning is just use, and use can vary between individual speakers or across historical periods, then there seems to be no fact of the matter about whether two speakers mean the same thing by a word, or whether we mean the same thing by 'democracy' as people in ancient Athens did. Some philosophers have sought to address this by distinguishing between the linguistic meaning of an expression (shared by competent speakers of a language) and speaker meaning (what a particular individual intends to convey in a specific utterance). Semantic theory can then concern itself with the former -- a stable, shared content -- while acknowledging the latter's irreducibly contextual character and the inevitable gap between what a speaker means and what a sentence means.

None of this need force an exclusive choice between the two pictures. A mature semantics may well be pluralistic, allowing that proper names and natural-kind terms lean heavily on reference while connectives, indexicals, and evaluative vocabulary are better explained by the rules governing their use. What the twentieth-century debate established is less the triumph of one theory than the inadequacy of assuming that a single mechanism must underwrite meaning across the whole of a language. The more durable lesson is methodological: before asking what a word means, one does well to ask what kind of word it is, since expressions of different types may secure their significance in quite different ways.
